hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4365.context: Arjuna explains his divine birth story, mentioning the sun and his mother Kunti.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4366.meaning: Trust in your journey. Even when things seem scattered, a higher power guides you to safety.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4366.context: Arjuna reflects on his birth and how Krishna has guided him through life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4367.meaning: It is okay to ask for what you need. Seek support for your home, work, and heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4367.context: Arjuna asks Krishna for a chariot, a home, and the love of Radha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4368.meaning: Respect your parents and those who raised you. Loyalty and love are key to strong bonds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4368.context: Arjuna says he knows his father and will always give him friendship and respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4473.meaning: Even in chaos, some people stay calm and pure, showing that inner peace can exist during hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4473.context: Krishna sees Gandhivi and Dhananjaya riding a white chariot while the battle fire burns brightly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4474.meaning: Trusting in a higher power or strong leadership can give you confidence when facing big challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4474.context: A warrior tells Krishna he is sure the enemy will be defeated in the coming battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4475.meaning: Preparing yourself with care and respect shows you take your duties seriously and honor your role.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4475.context: Three great warriors wear white clothes and garlands, showing they are ready for the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4476.meaning: True strength is not just about power, but also about how you carry yourself with dignity and grace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4476.context: A strong warrior rides a fine chariot under large white umbrellas, looking like a powerful tiger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4477.meaning: Sometimes, standing out with bold choices helps you show your true identity and commitment to your side.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4477.context: Krishna sees three famous warriors wearing red robes, which makes them stand out in the crowd.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4479.meaning: Experienced leaders working together can provide stability and wisdom, even when younger people are fighting.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4479.context: Old warriors and kings ride together on a camel, showing unity among the older generation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4480.meaning: Knowing where you are going helps you stay focused, even if the destination feels scary or final.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4480.context: The army moves toward a specific place, knowing they are heading toward a final judgment.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4481.meaning: When a group shares the same goal, their combined belief makes the outcome feel certain and inevitable.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4481.context: Kings and warriors gather together, confident that they will witness the great battle soon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4541.meaning: When you serve others with full heart, your efforts are never wasted, even if the path feels hard.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4541.context: A warrior feels torn by duty and desire, wondering if his actions for the king are truly worth it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4542.meaning: True worship means letting go of anger and showing deep respect to the divine every single day.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4542.context: Devotees worship the divine daily, dropping all hatred, and bow down with deep respect and humility.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4543.meaning: Even in conflict, deep connections make it hard to hurt those who truly care about your well-being.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4543.context: Enemies who share a bond with the speaker wonder how he could possibly break their strong wishes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4544.meaning: A true leader stays with their people through hard times, helping them reach their highest goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4544.context: The speaker sees himself as a guide helping others cross a difficult battle, refusing to leave them behind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4545.meaning: Sometimes you must put your own safety aside to protect what matters most to you and your people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4545.context: The warrior decides to sacrifice his own safety to protect the king, accepting his fate without fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4546.meaning: Ignoring your responsibilities when it matters most leads to confusion and bad consequences for your soul.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4546.context: People who are comfortable ignore their duties, and careless actions lead to chaos and spiritual trouble.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4547.meaning: Deep betrayal and evil acts have no place in a good afterlife, so we must choose kindness and honesty.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4547.context: The text describes severe sins, like betrayal, and warns that there is no good afterlife for such people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4548.meaning: Face your challenges with full honesty and strength, never hiding your true power or intentions from others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_4548.context: The warrior promises to fight the enemy sons honestly, using his full strength without lying or hiding.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5066.meaning: Being mean and hating kindness leads to bad arguments and trouble with older people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5066.context: A speaker describes a cruel person who hates good deeds and argues too much.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5067.meaning: You will soon see the heavy price you pay for your intense and bad choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5067.context: A speaker tells Duryodhana that he will soon see the results of his actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5068.meaning: Anger can make you question why good people are still alive in a confusing world.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5068.context: A speaker addresses Krishna with anger, questioning why he is alive in a foolish land.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5069.meaning: Losing your family and home brings deep disappointment and sadness to your life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5069.context: A speaker warns that great warriors will fall and you will lose your kingdom and sons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5070.meaning: Your evil deeds will lead to your death after you watch your loved ones fall.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5070.context: A speaker tells Duryodhana he will die after seeing his brothers and sons die first.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5071.meaning: Krishna always keeps his word, so you can trust that the truth will happen.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5071.context: A speaker assures that Krishna will keep his promise and the truth will come to pass.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5072.meaning: Sometimes the best response is to listen, accept the truth, and walk away calmly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5072.context: Kaitava hears the king's words, agrees with them, and quietly leaves the place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5073.meaning: Sharing what you hear with your group can help everyone understand the situation better.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5073.context: Duryodhana hides from the Pandavas and tells the Kuru assembly everything he heard.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5376.meaning: She seeks permission to leave, hoping the king will support her spiritual journey and hard work.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5376.context: A woman asks the king to let her travel abroad to practice hard ascetic rituals.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5377.meaning: She believes her past sins caused her current suffering, showing that actions have lasting effects.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5377.context: She reflects on past mistakes and feels the consequences of her earlier wrong actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5378.meaning: She is upset because she was turned away, and she struggles to find a place to belong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5378.context: She feels rejected by the ascetics and cannot return to her community with them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5379.meaning: She wants spiritual help to purify herself and grow closer to divine qualities.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5379.context: She asks for guidance to cleanse her sins and become more godlike through ascetic practice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5380.meaning: Through reassurance, they find peace and keep working together, showing support helps overcome doubt.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5380.context: He comforts a young woman with explanations, and they both continue their work with priests.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5381.meaning: Bhishma encourages action, and wise people consider the best way to assist her in need.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5381.context: Bhishma tells the ascetics to act, while righteous men debate how to help the girl.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5382.meaning: Different groups propose solutions, showing that many people care about his safety and future.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5382.context: Some ascetics suggest taking the girl home, while heavenly beings think about protecting him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5383.meaning: They debate his next step, noting that past rejection may affect his future opportunities.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5383.context: Others think he should work for Chalvapati, but some reject the idea because of past rejection.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5460.meaning: She shows deep respect and devotion, honoring Rama with humble, pure gestures.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5460.context: A noble woman bows before Rama, touching him with hands like lotus flowers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5461.meaning: Her sorrow is eased by trusting others, learning that sharing feelings brings relief.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5461.context: She weeps, eyes full of tears, while seeking comfort from another, finding joy in Bhrigu.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5462.meaning: He seeks divine aid to escape pain, trusting the Lord to rescue him from hardship.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5462.context: Ambo prays to the Lord, asking for help from sorrowful mud and a great promise.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5464.meaning: Bhishma’s strength inspires, but Rama fears his own responsibilities and the future.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5464.context: Bhishma sees hope, beauty, and age, feeling renewed, yet Rama worries about him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5466.meaning: Honesty and openness build trust, encouraging clear communication between friends.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5466.context: She smiles and tells Rama truthfully, inviting Bhrigu to share everything honestly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5467.meaning: He guides her, showing that wise counsel helps make important choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5467.context: Jamadagni hears the princess’s words and speaks to the determined lady about decisions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5468.meaning: Obeying promises is vital; breaking them leads to conflict and danger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5468.context: Jahni’s son must follow his words or face battle, warned by a gentle lady.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5470.meaning: Decisions can pause conflict, but readiness to act remains crucial for protection.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_5_5470.context: A princess stops actions, while a hero named Chalvapati is ready to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_29.meaning: True power comes from inner steadiness, not from what others say or how old you are.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_29.context: A warrior shows calm, not worried by others, using yoga, strength, enthusiasm, and age.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_31.meaning: Respect for life means avoiding unnecessary violence and protecting oneself with proper means.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_31.context: He stays united with others, refuses to fight without weapons or armor.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_32.meaning: Inner peace protects you from external noise and fear, keeping you calm in battle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_32.context: He will not be defeated by drums, conches, or any weapon sounds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_33.meaning: Even in conflict, people can pause, reflect, and see each other as more than enemies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_33.context: They arranged a meeting with the Kurus and Pandavas, looking at each other amazed.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_34.meaning: Wisdom and courage inspire others, turning fear into confidence and joy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_34.context: Great souls entered the city, soldiers around them were cheerful and hopeful.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_35.meaning: Knowledge and learning are honored, showing that learning brings respect and honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_35.context: In the evening, a sage praised Vayas, son of Satyavati, for his Veda knowledge.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_36.meaning: Awareness of time helps prepare for danger and understand the larger plan of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_36.context: A warning of a terrible battle, the Lord sees past, present, future.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_37.meaning: Sharing wisdom can heal sorrow and guide people toward peace and strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_37.context: He shared a secret with a powerful king, then brought his grieving sons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_272.meaning: When we chase strong desires, we can destroy ourselves and others, even if we look good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_272.context: A story about white people who are beautiful, but their strong desires cause destruction.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_273.meaning: Long life can bring joy, but true happiness comes from a cheerful heart, not just years.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_273.context: A king is told that people live happily for many years, about ten thousand years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_274.meaning: We can find wealth and courage by staying positive and respecting nature’s spirits.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_274.context: The king hears that followers of nature spirits are rich and that brave men stay cheerful.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_276.meaning: Longevity is not the same for everyone; we should value each life’s unique length.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_276.context: A king is praised for living eleven thousand years, while others live fifteen hundred years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_277.meaning: Nature’s names and places remind us that the world is connected and full of wonder.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_277.context: The king learns that the mountain’s north side ends at the sea, called Airavata.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_280.meaning: Some beings live beyond normal limits, showing that light can keep us alive and bright.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_280.context: The sun does not burn them, and they do not age; the moon and stars shine like ghosts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_281.meaning: True purity comes when we control our senses, even if we face hunger and hardship.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_281.context: They are not lively or fragrant, they are hungry, but they have conquered their senses.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_283.meaning: Great leaders can inspire long, strong lives, but we must use that time wisely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_283.context: The king is told he lives thirteen thousand years, and the best of his people live the longest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_500.meaning: Leaders must understand why their team fails and take responsibility for the outcome of difficult challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_500.context: Duryodhana asks his generals why they failed to defeat the powerful Pandava warriors during the fierce battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_501.meaning: Great efforts can create overwhelming power that changes the situation completely for everyone involved in the conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_501.context: The sound of arrows flying through the air was loud like wind and covered the sky like a cloud.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_503.meaning: True skill and focus can make a person seem unstoppable and powerful when facing great opposition.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_503.context: Arjuna fought with such intense power that he seemed like a divine being wielding thunderbolts against his enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_504.meaning: When danger surrounds you from all sides, you must stay calm and find a way to survive.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_504.context: The battlefield was filled with a terrifying sea of arrows and weapons that were impossible to escape or avoid.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_505.meaning: Conflict often causes great suffering for everyone involved, so peace is always the better and safer choice.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_505.context: Soldiers and animals were overwhelmed by the fighting and many were destroyed by the relentless attacks of the heroes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_506.meaning: Loyalty means working hard to protect those you care about, even when the task is very difficult.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_506.context: Bhishma performed great deeds in battle to protect Duryodhana and ensure his safety and success in the war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_507.meaning: We should always recognize and appreciate the people who stand by us and offer their protection and support.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_507.context: Duryodhana wonders which brave warriors stood guard on the right side of Bhishma to protect him from attacks.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_509.meaning: Every role in a team matters, and neglecting your duty can leave others vulnerable to harm and danger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_509.context: The king asks who failed to guard the north side of Bhishma while the other heroes were busy fighting.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_542.meaning: Even the strongest can fall; respect bravery and remember that war brings sorrow to all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_542.context: Bhishma, a great warrior, is killed by enemies during the great war of Kurukshetra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_543.meaning: They show respect and ask for his guidance, hoping to learn from his wisdom before he leaves.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_543.context: Duryodhana, Karna, Shakuni, and Saubala speak to Bhishma as he dies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_544.meaning: War is chaotic and frightening, reminding us that violence destroys peace and safety.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_544.context: The battlefield is filled with horses, elephants, and many weapons, creating a terrifying scene.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_545.meaning: He wants to understand the outcome, showing that knowledge is important even after conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_545.context: Bhishma asks Sanjaya to explain what happened after the battle and who won.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_547.meaning: He shows that breaking promises causes inner turmoil and that we must seek forgiveness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_547.context: Bhishma feels restless, saying he has broken his vows and mourns his father's bad deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_548.meaning: He warns that anger can spread like fire, urging calm and careful actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_548.context: Bhishma speaks to Sanjaya, saying his son caused him pain and comparing it to fire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_549.meaning: He wants to heal wounds and learn lessons, showing the value of understanding past mistakes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_549.context: Bhishma says he will remove the sorrow caused by Duryodhana and asks Sanjaya to explain everything.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_551.meaning: He stresses the need for clear knowledge so that leaders can act wisely and avoid future conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_551.context: Bhishma questions if the earth's rulers understand the battle, asking Sanjaya for details.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_626.meaning: Leaders must stand firm and guide their people with strength and confidence during difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_626.context: The king of Magadha leads his army with a special chariot and a bull in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_627.meaning: True power often comes from kindness and patience rather than just force or loud displays of anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_627.context: Divine compassion hides the truth while autumn clouds gather strength for the opposing side in the war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_628.meaning: Courage and shining character help you stand out and inspire others when facing great challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_628.context: Anik stands bravely at the front while Jayadratha shines brightly with silver armor in the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_630.meaning: Even the strongest forces need protection and guidance to keep their purpose safe and clear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_630.context: The lord of the seas protects the white deer symbol while the army shows its great power.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_631.meaning: Preparation and visible strength can intimidate opponents and show that you are ready for any task.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_631.context: Huge elephants roar like mountains while carrying spears and banners that show their readiness for battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_633.meaning: Honor and dignity are shown through how we carry ourselves and respect our traditions daily.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_633.context: Kalingapa shines with a tree symbol and is covered with an umbrella and other royal items.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_634.meaning: Self control allows you to remain calm and powerful even when surrounded by chaos and confusion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_634.context: Ketuman rides an elephant with great control and stands in battle like the sun behind clouds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_635.meaning: A clear and bright mind helps you move forward with purpose while others may retreat.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_635.context: Bhagadatta rides the best elephant with a shining mind while the king Vajradhara moves away.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_779.meaning: When enemies appear, be ready to defend yourself and your allies with courage and quick action.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_779.context: Young warriors of Dhritarashtra see a monkey banner, weapons drop, Pandavas prepare to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_780.meaning: Good leaders plan carefully, placing their resources in the best spot for success.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_780.context: A king tells Hrishikesh to position the chariot amid the soldiers of the army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_781.meaning: Friendship and loyalty motivate us to stand together and face challenges together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_781.context: A warrior says he will fight if he sees his friends ready to battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_782.meaning: Unity against wrong helps protect good and bring justice to those who harm others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_782.context: Someone watches others join the fight to defeat the evil-minded Dhritarashtra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_783.meaning: Strategic positioning strengthens a team, making it harder for enemies to attack.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_783.context: Hrishikesh and Gudakesh command the chariot to be placed in the middle of the army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_784.meaning: Family and friends support each other, especially when facing difficult decisions or battles.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_784.context: A father-in-law and a gentleman are friends; Kaunteya stands with his relatives after review.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_787.meaning: Even in sadness, we can find hope and courage when we share our fears with trusted friends.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_787.context: A man, depressed, speaks to Krishna as the army approaches, eager to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_788.meaning: Physical and emotional stress is normal, but staying calm helps us perform better.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_788.context: A person feels tired, thirsty, and nervous before a big event.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1475.meaning: Silence can show deep respect and inner strength when facing difficult choices or powerful opponents in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1475.context: Yudhisthira stays silent while his brothers speak to him during the tense moments before the great war begins.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1476.meaning: True wisdom allows you to see through others' masks and understand their hearts without saying much.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1476.context: Krishna speaks to the warriors with a calm smile, showing he understands their hidden fears and true intentions clearly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1477.meaning: Gathering wise and strong allies through persuasion is key to success in any major challenge.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1477.context: Krishna lists the great teachers and warriors who have been persuaded to join the fight on their side.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1478.meaning: Always seek guidance and try peaceful solutions before engaging in conflict to maintain honor and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1478.context: Ancient rules state that fighting without first trying to persuade your elders or teachers is a serious mistake.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1479.meaning: Following moral guidelines and respecting wisdom gives you confidence and a strong chance of winning.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1479.context: Krishna believes that following scriptural rules and respecting elders ensures victory in the upcoming battle for his side.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1480.meaning: Strategic positioning and calm confidence can intimidate opponents and shift the balance of power.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1480.context: Krishna positions his forces around the enemy army, creating a sense of awe and fear among the opposing soldiers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1481.meaning: Even strong leaders feel fear and should seek shelter and advice from those with more experience.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1481.context: King Yudhisthira approaches the great warrior Bhishma with fear, seeking protection and guidance from his respected elders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1483.meaning: Showing fear does not make you weak, but society often judges courage by outward actions alone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1483.context: Critics question Yudhisthira's bravery because he showed fear, suggesting he does not act like a true warrior.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1627.meaning: Even strong fighters can get hurt, showing that no one is truly safe in a big fight.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1627.context: Two warriors fought fiercely, with one hero hitting the other in the arm and jaw.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1628.meaning: Pride can make people fight harder, but it also makes the conflict much more dangerous.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1628.context: A huge battle started where proud warriors fought with great strength and fierce determination.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1629.meaning: Anger can make a person act like a roaring lion, causing great destruction around them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1629.context: A warrior named Dhrishtaketu got very angry and shot many arrows at his enemy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1630.meaning: When anger takes over, a person might act wildly and without thinking about the consequences.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1630.context: Dhrishtaketu was furious and released a storm of arrows at the enemy called Bahlika.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1631.meaning: Quick reactions in anger can be powerful, but they often lack careful thought or control.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1631.context: Chedirajas got angry and quickly shot nine arrows at his opponent during the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1632.meaning: Holding onto anger keeps the fight going, making it hard for anyone to find peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1632.context: Two angry warriors kept roaring and fighting each other with intense rage in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1633.meaning: Even the most scary or cruel people can be stopped by someone who is brave and strong.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1633.context: A cruel demon named Ghatotkacha fought, but another warrior named Alambusa stopped his attacks.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1634.meaning: Skill and cleverness can help you overcome a much stronger or more powerful opponent.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1634.context: Alambusa fought against the mighty Bhimasena and used bent arrows to stop his progress.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1656.meaning: Even small creatures can cause trouble, but wise people keep calm and use skillful actions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1656.context: During a battle, a bird attacked another, while Vayadarana, known for wise arrows, watched.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1657.meaning: True leaders honor brave fighters, showing respect for courage and strength in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1657.context: Sudakshina, a king, praised Kamboja warrior Sharutakarma, who fought bravely against a strong enemy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1658.meaning: Anger can lead to harsh actions; wise people should control emotions before acting.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1658.context: Sharutakarma, a skilled charioteer, became angry and fired many arrows, tearing his opponent apart.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1660.meaning: Facing anger, one can rise again, proving that courage grows through repeated challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1660.context: Iravan grew angry at Sharutayusha, fought again, and showed even greater bravery in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1661.meaning: Losses in war can shock everyone, reminding us that battles bring unexpected sorrow.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1661.context: Arjuna, a great charioteer, killed his horse during battle, causing a loud roar among soldiers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1662.meaning: Violence often starts with a single act, showing how quickly battles can spread.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1662.context: Sharutayusa, enraged, struck a horse with a club during the Phalguni battle, sparking conflict.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1663.meaning: Strong leaders ready their people, emphasizing teamwork and readiness for upcoming challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1663.context: Vindanuvindava and Avantya, charioteers of Kuntibhoja, prepared their army and brave son for war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1664.meaning: Consistent effort and teamwork lead to success, even against powerful opponents.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1664.context: The Avantis displayed great skill, fighting steadily with a large army in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1636.meaning: Great power can hurt both sides, showing that even the strongest can be wounded in conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1636.context: Two warriors got hurt by arrows during a fierce fight that looked like gods fighting demons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1638.meaning: Retaliation often leads to more pain, as each side tries to win by hurting the other.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1638.context: A warrior hit his enemy with a sharp arrow, and another fighter struck back hard.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1639.meaning: Violence escalates quickly when people use deadly weapons, leading to mutual destruction and loss.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1639.context: Fighters used very sharp arrows to kill each other in a chaotic and deadly battlefield scene.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1640.meaning: Leadership and courage are vital when facing danger, as they guide the group through chaos.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1640.context: A brave hero and a strong army commander led their troops into a quick attack.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1641.meaning: Skill and focus are needed in conflict, but constant attacks can lead to endless cycles of harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1641.context: A warrior named Kripa shot many arrows at his enemy on the open battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1642.meaning: Anger makes people destroy useful things, showing how rage ruins tools and causes unnecessary damage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1642.context: Angry warriors shot arrows at each other, killing horses and breaking bows in the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1645.meaning: When tools fail, people must face their fears directly, revealing their true strength and courage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1645.context: Two strong fighters dropped their chariots and fought hand to hand with swords.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1646.meaning: Parents feel joy in their children's strength, hoping they will grow up to be brave and successful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1646.context: A king was happy about his son Jayadratha, who looked strong and cheerful in the story.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_6_1681.meaning: Chaos and violence destroy order and peace. We must see how conflict divides people and causes great suffering in the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2284.meaning: Lord Krishna's divine intervention saves Arjuna from a dangerous situation. It reminds us of the power of faith in the divine.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2614.meaning: Even when we mock others, we can still be wise and powerful if we use our skills responsibly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2614.context: Partha laughed at others, yet he was a wise teacher and a skilled archer in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2616.meaning: Strong leaders can be defeated, and danger can be avoided by staying alert and careful.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2617.context: Arjuna used his arrows to defeat Kritavarma and rode young horses toward the Kamboja region.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2619.meaning: Respecting others and acknowledging their strength builds peace and shows humility in conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2619.context: Arjuna gave Sudakshina to Kritavarma and praised the Kamboja warriors, describing Darona as a mountain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2620.meaning: Consistent effort and courage help achieve goals, even when facing the same challenges repeatedly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2620.context: Arjuna again used arrows to defeat Kritavarma and rode young horses toward the Kamboja lands.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2622.meaning: Giving thanks and recognizing others’ worth creates harmony and respect among people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2622.context: Arjuna paid Sudakshina to Kritavarma and honored Kamboja fighters, calling Darona a mountain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2623.meaning: Persistence and bravery can lead to success, even when the same task repeats.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2623.context: Arjuna used arrows to defeat Kritavarma and rode young horses toward the Kamboja territory again.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2626.meaning: Honoring others and acknowledging their strength helps maintain peace and mutual respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2626.context: Arjuna gave Sudakshina to Kritavarma and praised Kamboja warriors, describing Darona as a mountain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2721.meaning: War brings deep sorrow and pain to everyone involved, showing how terrible violence truly is for all life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2721.context: The battlefield looks dark and terrible because blood covers the entire earth surface completely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2722.meaning: Death takes many lives in war, reminding us that fighting causes great loss for families and society.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2722.context: Many warriors fall in battle, representing the great loss of life during this huge war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2723.meaning: Violence destroys strong people quickly, showing that no one is safe from the sudden shock of war.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2723.context: Soldiers lie dead on the ground, pierced by many arrows, looking like mountains hit by lightning.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2724.meaning: When duty calls, one must act with great strength and focus, even if it feels chaotic and intense.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2724.context: Arjuna fights fiercely, destroying horses and chariots, moving through the battle like a wild elephant.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2725.meaning: Anger and conflict spread fast, destroying peace and nature, so we must stop fires before they grow.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2725.context: Fire burns through the forest trees and grass, spreading quickly like the wind blowing through dry fuel.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2726.meaning: Hatred fuels violence like fire, causing more destruction, so we should choose peace over angry revenge.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2727.meaning: Skill and grace can exist in hard times, showing that doing your duty well brings honor and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2727.context: Arjuna moves gracefully in battle, his chariot empty of enemies, shining with glory like a skilled dancer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2728.meaning: Powerful actions can change the course of events, but anger must be controlled to avoid unnecessary harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2728.context: Arjuna shoots arrows like thunder, making the ground shake as he enters the enemy army with rage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2905.meaning: The battle was fierce and chaotic, showing how power and technology can make war overwhelming and destructive.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2905.context: Warriors used elephants, horses, and men, fighting with birds and charioteers pulling bows the size of palm trees.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2906.meaning: The war left many casualties, reminding us that conflict brings loss and suffering to all involved.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2906.context: Swords, skins, bows, heads, and shields were scattered among the great heroes in the battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2907.meaning: The violence was brutal, illustrating how war can strip humanity and reduce people to mere trophies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2907.context: They ate meat, drank blood, and even took parts of the king's hair and marrow during the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2910.meaning: The scene shows the grim reality of war, where lives are taken and bodies become symbols of defeat.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2910.context: Bodies and body parts were attracted; heads of men, horses, and elephants were cut down in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2911.meaning: Their determination shows how people fight for honor, but also how such battles can lead to great loss.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2911.context: Armed with weapons, they entered battle, wielding bows, fighting fiercely for victory.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2912.meaning: The variety of weapons shows the complexity of war, where many tactics are used to try to win.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2912.context: They marched in many ways with spears, powers, and javelins in the battle of Tawaka.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2913.meaning: The fighting turned into mutual destruction, teaching that war often harms both sides and destroys peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2913.context: Some used clubs and spears, others used different arms; angry men killed each other on the battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2914.meaning: Their fierce actions show how war can turn people into enemies, causing pain and conflict among allies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_2914.context: Kashibas and Charanas fought in the arena, screaming and kicking each other during the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3149.meaning: True joy comes from peace and victory, not from anger or fighting with others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3149.context: Arjuna feels happy and calm after the Pandavas win a big battle against their enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3150.meaning: Seeing others happy can make us feel sad when our own family faces hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3150.context: The Kauravas watch the Pandavas smiling at each other, feeling sad about their own sons' fate.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3151.meaning: Fear often makes us believe the worst things are true before we know the facts.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3151.context: People traveled to the Kuru camp, thinking their son had been eaten by a fierce god.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3152.meaning: Sudden loss can cause panic, but we must stay calm and trust in what is right.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3152.context: Warriors saw the king was gone and shouted in fear, telling Krishna and the Pandavas.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3153.meaning: Anger and revenge only lead to more pain and destruction for everyone involved.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3153.context: Duryodhana heard the crowd screaming and vowed to kill the two Krishnas in revenge.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3154.meaning: Real sacrifice is about giving up ego and serving others with a pure heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3154.context: A speaker asks Arjuna to show the true sacrifice that connects divine and human life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3156.meaning: We should act with courage and confidence when facing difficult challenges in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3156.context: The speaker challenges Arjuna to show his strength and manliness quickly in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3157.meaning: We should recognize and honor those who act with kindness, truth, and good character.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3157.context: The speaker asks to see the people who are truly worthy of honor and respect.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3215.meaning: Loud actions can shake the world around us, showing how one person can affect everyone nearby.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3216.meaning: Calling for help or hope can lift spirits and give strength when things seem very dark.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3217.meaning: True skill and confidence allow you to overcome obstacles with ease and grace in life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3232.meaning: Focused effort can disable strong opponents, showing that determination breaks through even the toughest barriers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3233.meaning: Using the right tools and sharp focus helps you solve difficult problems effectively and quickly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3233.context: Arjuna uses his sword and fiery arrows to strike down several powerful warriors in combat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3234.meaning: Persistence in your goals ensures you keep moving forward despite the number of challenges you face.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3234.context: Arjuna continues his attack, hitting Gautama and Shaindhava with many arrows in the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3235.meaning: Anger can drive people to fight back hard, but it often leads to more conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3235.context: An angry warrior named Bhuri Shavaras attacks Arjuna with many arrows after seeing his allies fall.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3236.meaning: Overwhelming effort can stop opposition in its tracks, protecting what matters most to you.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3301.meaning: Great skill can stop a huge attack, showing that one strong person can change the whole fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3302.meaning: Anger can make a person feel incredibly powerful, but it also makes them very scary to others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3303.meaning: Victory can bring great joy, and a strong leader's confidence can feel like saving everyone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3306.meaning: Quick action is needed when danger comes, and using the right tool can stop a serious threat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_3307.meaning: After a big fight, you must move quickly to support your team and keep the battle going.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_4549.meaning: Anger makes people act without thinking, causing more harm than good to everyone involved.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_4555.meaning: In difficult times, we need to stay focused and protect those who stand beside us.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_4660.meaning: Pain and injury do not have to stop you from standing firm in your purpose.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6158.meaning: Unity and loud confidence can intimidate opponents and show that a group stands together firmly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6159.meaning: Passion and enthusiasm give us the power to overcome difficult challenges and face our fears.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6160.meaning: Losing control of your emotions can make you act foolishly and dangerously in serious situations.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6160.context: Kritavarma attacks Yudhisthira with wild intensity, acting like a drunk person trying to kill Darona.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6161.meaning: Facing a large group requires focus and steady action to protect yourself from overwhelming odds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6161.context: Shaineya shoots many arrows while the Kaurava army attacks in large numbers at the front lines.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6162.meaning: Preparation and skill are essential tools that help us succeed when we face strong competition.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6162.context: Sahadeva and other great warriors prepare their chariots and weapons to fight against the enemy forces.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6163.meaning: Vitality and strength can lead to victory, but arrogance often leads to a person's downfall.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6163.context: Bhima fights with youthful energy while Duryodhana meets his end in the midst of the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6164.meaning: Being skilled and quick to act allows you to handle threats effectively and protect your side.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6164.context: Nakula shows his skill as a warrior and quickly stops the enemy fighter named Saubala.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6598.meaning: Sometimes you need special help to overcome a strong enemy. Trust in divine support when facing difficult challenges in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6598.context: Krishna advises Arjuna to kill Karna using divine help, comparing it to a past mythological event involving Indra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6599.meaning: Confidence in your own strength is important. You are capable of handling tough situations with the right mindset.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6599.context: Arjuna declares his confidence in defeating Karna and Drona, noting that other warriors are also ready to fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6600.meaning: Do your duty without fear or favoritism. Justice must be served equally to everyone, no matter who they are.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6600.context: Arjuna vows to kill all enemies regardless of their status, following the strict path of duty and righteousness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6601.meaning: Anger can make you look scary and dangerous. Keep your cool to avoid making mistakes in heated moments.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6601.context: Karna looks angry and fierce like a serpent in the dark, while his charioteer prepares for the intense battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6604.meaning: Conflicts can be loud and chaotic. Stay focused on your goal even when the situation seems overwhelming and scary.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6604.context: A fierce night battle erupts between two powerful warriors, with sounds like roaring tigers echoing through the darkness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6605.meaning: React quickly to threats but stay aware of your surroundings. Sudden changes require immediate and careful attention.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6605.context: Karna sees Ghatotkacha crossing his chariot and draws his sword to fight him during the chaotic night battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6606.meaning: Seek help from allies when you are surrounded. Teamwork and strategic movement can turn the tide in your favor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6606.context: Krishna urges Arjuna to stop Karna, who is surrounded by a large army, and move to where Rama is.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6608.meaning: Even strong warriors need protection and support. Ask for help when you are facing many opponents alone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_6608.context: Karna fights fiercely in battle, and the speaker asks for protection for him as he faces the enemy army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7295.meaning: Anger often leads to rash actions that cause harm. We must control our temper to avoid making mistakes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7295.context: A warrior shoots arrows in anger at his enemy during a fierce battle scene in the epic war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7296.meaning: Skill and speed can help you overcome threats. Stay focused and act decisively when danger is near.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7296.context: A hero rides his chariot and quickly defeats several opponents who were chasing him closely during the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7297.meaning: True strength shines even in difficult times. Your character matters more than your current situation or appearance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7297.context: Nakula drives a damaged chariot that looks majestic and powerful like a god standing on a mountain peak.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7298.meaning: Duty sometimes forces us to oppose those we respect. Honor your role even when it feels hard.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7298.context: Two skilled warriors, a teacher and his student, face each other in battle with their weapons ready.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7299.meaning: Great events capture everyone's attention. Pause to observe important moments and learn from the actions of others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7299.context: All the soldiers stop fighting to watch the unique battle between the teacher and his student closely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7301.meaning: Life brings strange and difficult challenges. Trust your abilities even when the situation seems impossible to handle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7301.context: Two brothers fight a great battle that seems impossible and strange, like finding food while lying in the sky.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7303.meaning: Confidence helps you stay calm under pressure. Do not let your opponent's efforts discourage your own resolve.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7303.context: One warrior tries hard to win but his opponent laughs and strikes back quickly with great skill.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7304.meaning: When direct paths fail, adapt your strategy. Use your skills wisely to protect yourself and your allies.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7304.context: When one warrior cannot defeat his rival, he uses a special weapon to attack the other fighters nearby.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7803.meaning: Strong actions often come from trusted advice. We should listen to wise mentors when facing difficult or urgent situations.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7803.context: Bhima jumps from his chariot to grab a woman after getting encouragement from his father Vasudeva.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7804.meaning: Anger can lead to rash actions. We must pause and think before reacting violently to what we see.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7804.context: The Pandavas see Satyaki and become angry. One warrior grabs his weapon and forces his way to Bali.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7805.meaning: When injustice happens, speak up clearly. Silence allows wrongs to continue while brave voices can stop them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7805.context: A warrior jumps down and sees someone being carried away. Sahadeva speaks sharply to address the situation immediately.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7807.meaning: True friendship crosses all social lines. We should value loyal companions regardless of their background or origin.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7807.context: A speaker tells Krishna that their friend is from the Andhaka and Panchala groups, showing deep loyalty.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7808.meaning: Loyalty is rare and precious. Recognize those who stand by you through thick and thin without hesitation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7808.context: The speaker emphasizes that among the Andhakas and Vrishnis, Krishna has no friend more loyal than this one.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7809.meaning: Be a reliable friend to others. When you are trustworthy, people will naturally look to you for help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7809.context: Addressing Krishna, the speaker says even the Panchalas see him as their only true friend and support.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7810.meaning: Friendship is a two way street. Mutual respect and care create strong bonds that last forever.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7810.context: The speaker explains that Krishna views them as true friends, just as they view him in the same way.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7811.meaning: Self control is a key virtue. Master your emotions to act with wisdom and kindness instead of rage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7811.context: Knowing all duties, the speaker urges Satyaki to control his anger toward the Panchala princess and calm down.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7921.meaning: True loyalty means rushing to help others even when you are scared or tired yourself.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7921.context: A tired warrior fought hard while Daraunim rushed forward to save his life from danger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7922.meaning: Even when trouble falls on you, keep your courage and do your duty with strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7922.context: Arrows rained down on the son of Darona while the great charioteer fought bravely in war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7923.meaning: Holding onto past hurts can make you act with rage instead of calm wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7923.context: Darauni felt deep anger in battle and shot ten arrows to avenge his fathers death.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7924.meaning: Preparation is important but using strength to hurt others brings pain to everyone involved.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7924.context: Warriors carried sharp weapons and strong bows to attack the king of Panchalas in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7925.meaning: Letting anger control your actions can lead to chaos and harm those around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7925.context: Daraunisha turned his chariot in anger and shot arrows at all his enemies in war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7926.meaning: Running from problems leaves you feeling empty and does not solve the real issue.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7926.context: The Panchala army ran away in fear while their leader looked sad and hurt by arrows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7927.meaning: Standing up for your friends when they are weak shows true bravery and loyalty.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7927.context: Seeing his friends retreat, Shainey quickly attacked Daraunis chariot to help his side in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7928.meaning: Violence often spreads quickly and causes more suffering for everyone involved in the conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_7_7928.context: He shot many arrows at the enemy and hit the charioteer with four horses in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_323.meaning: Loyalty and duty can sustain a cause even when the odds seem very difficult to overcome.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_323.context: The Pandavas fight bravely in the war while Bhishma protects their side for ten days.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_324.meaning: True strength comes from within and helps you guide others through tough challenges with confidence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_324.context: A warrior is praised for his strength and ability to lead armies with great skill.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_327.meaning: Loyalty and duty can sustain a cause even when the odds seem very difficult to overcome.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_327.context: The Pandavas fight bravely in the war while Bhishma protects their side for ten days.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_328.meaning: True strength comes from within and helps you guide others through tough challenges with confidence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_328.context: A warrior is praised for his strength and ability to lead armies with great skill.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_330.meaning: Faith in a higher power gives us the courage to face and overcome our biggest fears.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_330.context: A divine figure is asked to protect the army and defeat all enemies like a god.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_331.meaning: Knowing when to step back is wise and protects you from unnecessary harm or loss.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_331.context: Advice is given to withdraw the army when the situation becomes too dangerous or unclear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_332.meaning: Without clear guidance, people can feel lost and unable to work together effectively toward goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_332.context: The Pandavas are described as being in a state of confusion or lack of awareness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_333.meaning: Goodness and truth naturally dispel ignorance and fear, bringing peace and clarity to life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_333.context: The sun is compared to a warrior who removes darkness and defeats enemies with light.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_681.meaning: Even in violent conflict, people maintain their cultural identity and personal dignity through traditional symbols of honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_681.context: The text describes a warrior covered in sacred paste and wearing fine jewelry during the great war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_682.meaning: Human bodies are powerful instruments that can be adorned with beauty even while engaged in harsh struggles.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_682.context: The description highlights the physical strength and decorated limbs of the soldiers fighting on the battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_683.meaning: War destroys beautiful things and causes great suffering, reminding us that violence leaves a lasting mark.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_683.context: Broken chariots with golden bells and bloody horseshoes show the chaotic and destructive nature of the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_685.meaning: The repetition shows how war ruins valuable possessions and creates a scene of widespread destruction and pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_685.context: This verse repeats the image of shattered chariots and blood-soaked equipment to emphasize the intensity of combat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_686.meaning: The sound of war continues even as individuals fall, showing the relentless and impersonal nature of conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_686.context: Warriors blow conch shells while their fallen comrades lie on the ground like defeated elephants in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_687.meaning: Every individual life has value and name, and their death is a specific tragedy amidst the chaos.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_687.context: Specific elephant warriors are named as they are killed, highlighting the personal loss within the larger war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_688.meaning: The destruction extends to animals too, reminding us that war harms all living beings involved in it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_688.context: More elephant names are listed as their bells are crushed, showing the heavy toll on the war beasts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_689.meaning: Material wealth and symbols of power are fragile and can be lost quickly in the face of violence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_689.context: Precious gems and flags fall to the ground as the battle rages, symbolizing the loss of status.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_708.meaning: Strong confidence and bravery can make a warrior powerful, but pride may lead to trouble.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_708.context: Today the enemy hero shows great skill, learning, influence, courage, and pride.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_709.meaning: Confidence in battle can boost performance, but true strength comes from humility and skill.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_709.context: Darona, Bhishma, and others think they are the best fighters, even when finished.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_710.meaning: Everyone has worth; comparing oneself to others can hurt confidence and peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_710.context: Karna and Bhishma are equal, and neither wants to be less than Vasudeva or Arjuna.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_711.meaning: Strong teamwork and steady movement help a group win battles, just like a wheel turns smoothly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_711.context: A chariot, horse, and elephant fight like infantry, led by Pandya, moving like a potter’s wheel.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_713.meaning: Skillful shooting can create powerful effects, showing how precision helps in battle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_713.context: Vayashwa and others shoot arrows, making the wind look like clouds, while Pandya fights.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_714.meaning: Being a good rider gives a warrior advantage and confidence on the battlefield.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_714.context: Pulinda, Khash, and others are strong horsemen, fighting bravely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_716.meaning: Fearless fighting and strong words can inspire troops, but respect for all is important.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_716.context: The southern forces and Bhojas are fierce, using arrows, and Pandya shouts at the young.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_717.meaning: Facing many enemies can overwhelm, reminding us to stay calm and think clearly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_717.context: A four-armed army shoots arrows at Pandya, and Daraunir feels more confused and scared.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_860.meaning: Even powerful forces can be defeated quickly, reminding us that strength alone does not guarantee safety.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_860.context: Nakula's army was destroyed by arrows, causing chaos like clouds scattered by wind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_862.meaning: Observing events calmly helps us learn lessons without getting caught up in conflict.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_862.context: During the battle, divine arrows struck enemies, and the hero stepped back to watch.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_863.meaning: Showing off power can provoke others to fight back, leading to more danger for everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_863.context: Warriors showed their weapons, and the fight escalated toward mutual destruction.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_865.meaning: When danger approaches, people protect themselves, showing the need for caution in risky situations.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_865.context: Nakula fired arrows at a red robe, and the people covered their ears in the city.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_866.meaning: Material wealth can be hidden or absent, reminding us that true value lies beyond money.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_866.context: They entered a funeral hall, finding no money, and the king compared it to a hidden moon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_867.meaning: When enemies become more dangerous, we must stay alert and protect ourselves.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_867.context: Karuddha grew fierce, and arrows rained on the Pandavas during battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_868.meaning: Even bright hope can be dimmed by conflict, urging us to keep faith during hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_868.context: The Pandavas were attacked by Suta's son, and the sun seemed hidden by clouds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_869.meaning: Unpredictable actions can overwhelm others, teaching us to be careful with our choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_869.context: A laughing charioteer fired many arrows, sending hundreds and thousands into battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1636.meaning: When we lose something, we should remember that it is still part of us and can be found again.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1636.context: Ryan talks to a swan that has fallen, saying the lost swan is the one that fell.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1637.meaning: The world moves quickly, and we must be ready to follow the path that leads to peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1637.context: The swan flies west, and the sea belongs to Varuna, moving very fast.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1638.meaning: Fear can make us feel helpless, but we should look for hope even when things seem bad.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1638.context: A crow feels fear, falls, and sees trees fall, thinking it will drown in autumn water.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1639.meaning: Life is full of many people and ideas, and we should respect all of them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1639.context: The sea holds many beings, and the sky shines with many great beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1640.meaning: Even when we feel far from help, we can still listen and learn from the world around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1640.context: The sea is deep, and the clouds and waters are strong, but the crow's ears are far from water.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1641.meaning: When we see someone in trouble, we should try to help them find balance and peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1641.context: Seeing the swan decline, the swan says they want to lift the drowning Samarana Satpurushavrata.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1643.meaning: We should share what we know, so others can learn and avoid mistakes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1643.context: I have seen many falls, and if this is hidden, you are not telling us a secret.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1644.meaning: We can learn from our mistakes by trying again and staying connected to what matters.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_1644.context: The crow asks what the name of the fall is, and it touches water with wings again.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2070.meaning: When people stand together, they can face challenges and support each other, just like strong trees.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2070.context: A group of warriors is compared to trees shaken by wind, showing their unity and strength.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2071.meaning: Even powerful heroes can be defeated, reminding us that everyone faces danger and must be careful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2071.context: Bhima kills Karatha, who dies after being hit by a sharp arrow, falling to the ground.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2072.meaning: When people suffer, we should listen and help, showing compassion and courage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2072.context: A loud cry of distress is heard as the king’s soldiers are being killed by enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2073.meaning: Strong and brave leaders inspire others to fight for good and protect their people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2073.context: Bhimasena, Nanda, and Pananda are praised as the greatest warriors, shaking the enemy army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2074.meaning: Seeing great strength can scare people, but it also reminds us to respect powerful forces.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2074.context: Soldiers flee from Bhimasena, terrified by his battle power, and feel like time is ending.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2075.meaning: Loss can hurt deeply, yet victories show that perseverance can bring success.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2075.context: Suta’s son watches his own sons die while the Pandavas defeat a horse with a swan color.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2076.meaning: Quick action and support from allies help a leader face challenges and win battles.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2076.context: The king of Madras sends horses to Bhimasena’s chariot, preparing for battle quickly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2077.meaning: Even the most powerful enemies can be challenged, encouraging us to stand firm in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2077.context: Karna, a fierce warrior, fights the Pandavas in a chaotic and dangerous battlefield.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2078.meaning: Seeing powerful allies reminds us that important moments can change quickly if we stay alert.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2078.context: A king watches two great charioteers, realizing a big event will happen soon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2079.meaning: Even strong people can stumble; we must be careful and ready for unexpected challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2079.context: The king falls easily, striking a man without a chariot in a sudden attack.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2080.meaning: Pride and mockery can lead to downfall; humility keeps us safe in tough times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2080.context: A top warrior laughs at others, falling from a broken throne without a chariot.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2081.meaning: Facing a powerful foe teaches us to respect danger and prepare for fierce battles.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2081.context: A serpent king, not a toothless destroyer, appears angry and fierce against enemies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2082.meaning: Hidden emotions can hurt others; being honest helps avoid misunderstandings and pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2082.context: He has eyes around his teeth, a deep smile that feels painful and intense.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2083.meaning: Fear can spread quickly, but staying calm helps us see the way forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2083.context: They flee from the enemy, scared, and darkness covers the battlefield like clouds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2084.meaning: Using skill and timing can defeat even the strongest opponent if we act wisely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2084.context: A warrior strikes a serpent with a club, like wind blowing through clouds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2085.meaning: Strength can return after loss; remembering past victories gives hope for future success.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2085.context: The serpent’s son is strong again, and the first of the Kaunteyas is the fifty-fifth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2221.meaning: Even in war, a warrior can feel pain and loss, showing that conflict brings suffering.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2221.context: During a battle, a warrior’s body was covered with burning earrings, and he dropped his sword.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2223.meaning: Death ends a life, reminding us that all are part of the natural cycle and must return.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2223.context: A warrior’s head fell like meat, then his body hit the ground, and he was united with the earth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2224.meaning: Loss of a leader causes chaos, showing the importance of steady guidance for a group.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2224.context: When a great king died, his followers were shocked, fled in all directions, and left Gautama alone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2225.meaning: Powerful leaders can control conflict, and humility can prevent unnecessary fighting.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2225.context: Mighty Rama stopped Dhrishtadyumna in battle, while Kritavarma told an arrogant attendant to stay.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2226.meaning: Strong determination can lead to conflict, and anger can harm those close to us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2226.context: Dhrishtadyumna fought fiercely with nine arrows, while Ajaghanorasi angrily tormented his son.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2228.meaning: Even allies can cause harm, reminding us to be careful with those we trust.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2228.context: Kritavarma was badly wounded by his attendant, and they covered the chariot and horse with arrows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2229.meaning: When leaders are absent, uncertainty grows, and darkness can cover clarity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2229.context: The king noted Dhrishtadyumna was not seen on the chariot, and the sun was hidden by clouds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2230.meaning: Protecting what is valuable is hard, and battles can leave leaders injured.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_2230.context: Arrows were shot away from golden ornaments, and the king saw Dhrishtadyumna wounded in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3030.meaning: Fear can make warriors back away, even when they are strong and ready to fight.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3030.context: Panchalas fight bravely, but fear Adhiratha and retreat from battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3031.meaning: Speed and powerful weapons can surprise enemies and cause great damage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3031.context: Panchalas attack quickly, using arrows that burn like fire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3032.meaning: Old grudges can bring pain, and remembering them can hurt people today.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3032.context: Rama speaks about a weapon that hurts like a Bhrigu’s ear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3034.meaning: The battlefield can become overwhelming, making everyone feel scared and exhausted.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3034.context: All armies feel a hot, frightening heat that covers them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3035.meaning: Strong attacks can spread heat and danger, affecting many people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3035.context: Arrows fall from a bow, burning like bright fire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3036.meaning: When a strong weapon is used, it is hard for others to stop the attack.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3036.context: Panchalas move everywhere, using a powerful ear weapon in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3037.meaning: Strong emotions can be hurtful, and they can damage even the strongest people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3037.context: Arjuna feels a fierce anger, and sharp arrows pierce his ear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3038.meaning: Being part of many groups can cause confusion, and ignoring problems makes them worse.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3038.context: Pandavas are linked to both sides, and a neglected ear feels like illness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3193.meaning: True strength comes from loyalty and duty, even when facing powerful and dangerous opponents in battle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3193.context: Great warriors like Karna and Kripa fought bravely on the battlefield during the war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3194.meaning: Keeping your word builds trust and honor, showing that integrity matters more than just winning fights.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3194.context: The Pandavas performed a wonderful feat in battle, fulfilling their promises to their allies and friends.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3195.meaning: Observe the situation carefully before acting, as understanding the current state helps you make wise choices.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3195.context: Arjuna saw the enemy force defeated and wondered what Karna would do next in the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3197.meaning: Perseverance through hardship and heat leads to victory, showing that endurance is key to success.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3197.context: Karna fought fiercely in the hot afternoon, killing many soldiers while Bhima also defeated the enemy army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3199.meaning: Recognize danger early and seek support, because facing overwhelming odds alone often leads to failure.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3199.context: Seeing his army torn apart by Bhima, Karna warned his charioteer not to face the Panchalas alone.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3200.meaning: Using your natural talents and speed wisely allows you to overcome many challenges with confidence.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3200.context: King Shalya rode swift white horses and defeated many enemy groups with great strength and skill.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3201.meaning: Passion and drive can fuel great achievements, but they must be directed with purpose and focus.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3201.context: Shalya attacked the Pandava forces like a thirsty tiger, eager to claim victory in the great war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3203.meaning: Great events create powerful impacts, reminding us that our actions can shake the world around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3203.context: The loud roar of chariots echoed across the battlefield, sounding like thunder or cracking mountains.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3215.meaning: One strong person can face many foes if they stay brave and focused on the task.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3215.context: Karna fights many enemies alone in a fierce battle and shoots them with arrows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3216.meaning: Even the strongest heroes can lose, so we must stay humble and ready for change.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3216.context: A king hears news that Karna, a great hero, was defeated in the recent fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3217.meaning: Obstacles can block your path, but you must keep trying to move forward.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3217.context: The Pandavas and their king try to move forward but are stopped by enemy arrows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3218.meaning: True greatness comes from having a good heart and doing your best in hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3218.context: Gods and sages praise Karna for his great soul and his skill in the battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3219.meaning: Your unique talents are gifts that can help you stand out and serve others well.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3219.context: People call Karna the best charioteer and bowman, praising his amazing skills in war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3220.meaning: Anger can be destructive, so it is better to stay calm and control your emotions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3220.context: Karna burns the enemy army like a huge fire, showing his power and fierce anger.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3221.meaning: Fear makes people cry out, but staying calm helps you think clearly and act wisely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3221.context: The Panchalas cry out in fear as Karna shoots sharp arrows at them in the fight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3223.meaning: Intimidation can scare you, but knowing your own strength helps you overcome that fear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3223.context: The Pandava army is terrified by the loud sounds and sees Karna as a mighty warrior.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3292.meaning: True strength comes from facing many challenges and standing firm against all odds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3292.context: A warrior boasts about his past victories against many enemies in ancient times.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3293.meaning: When you honor the divine, you gain the inner power to overcome great difficulties.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3293.context: A hero pleases a great god and receives a powerful divine weapon for battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3294.meaning: Leaders should always recognize and reward the hard work of their loyal supporters.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3294.context: A king wins a battle in a city and rewards his loyal charioteers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3296.meaning: Trust in a higher power gives you the courage to face any enemy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3296.context: A warrior chooses a specific ally for battle, trusting in divine protection.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3297.meaning: Real bravery is having the skill and heart to handle tough situations calmly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3297.context: A general praises two brave warriors who can handle any strong weapon in war.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3299.meaning: Accepting your fate helps you act with total clarity and without fear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3299.context: A warrior accepts that he might die in battle but fights with full focus.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3300.meaning: Unity among strong people creates a powerful force that can achieve great things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3300.context: A king greets his son and lists the great warriors joining the army.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3301.meaning: Holding onto anger can drive you to act, but it is a heavy burden.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3301.context: A warrior vows to defeat two enemies who have caused him great pain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3363.meaning: Even the strongest warriors can be defeated, showing that no one is truly safe in war.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_8_3363.context: The king sees many enemy riders falling from their horses during the fierce battle.
