hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5924.context: The verse lists fiery attributes and says the divine is immortal and free from all sin.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5925.meaning: God is everywhere, from the tiniest atom to the biggest universe, and holds all good qualities.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5925.context: This part describes the divine as both very small and very large, holding all virtues.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5926.meaning: God is a safe place for the mind, granting wishes and guiding the spirit to peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5926.context: The text calls the divine a yogi who fulfills all desires and acts as a shelter.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5927.meaning: God keeps the world in order by controlling actions and ensuring that justice is always served.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_5927.context: The verse identifies the divine as a bowman and a restrainer who controls all actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6299.meaning: God has many different faces, some scary and some bright, to show his total power.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6299.context: The wise speak about the many scary and bright forms of the supreme being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6300.meaning: We use many names for God because he does so many big and powerful things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6300.context: The holy books list many names for the supreme being based on his great deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6301.meaning: The oldest and wisest people wrote the best prayers to honor the true divine power.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6301.context: Old sages in the Vedas praise the supreme being with their best and deepest words.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6302.meaning: God is the oldest and greatest source who gives life and energy to everything.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6302.context: Sages call the supreme being the eldest one who gives life to all worlds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6303.meaning: Sacred fire acts like a strong force that helps free people from their problems.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6303.context: Fire is described as the first horse born from the gods to free trapped souls.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6304.meaning: If you trust in God, he will give you a healthy, long, and happy life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6304.context: The supreme being gives long life, health, and wealth to those who trust him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6305.meaning: Even the strongest gods get their power from the one true supreme source.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6305.context: The supreme being gives power to gods like Indra and controls their strength.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6306.meaning: God is the master of all desires and wealth, controlling both good and bad outcomes.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6306.context: The supreme being is the greatest in all good and evil things in the world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6504.meaning: We must respect and honor our spiritual guides and teachers who help us grow in wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6504.context: A speaker angrily accuses a leader of harming priests and teachers during a heated debate.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6505.meaning: True strength is shown by staying calm and peaceful even when others are angry or upset.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6505.context: Bhishma finishes his speech to the warriors and sits down calmly while the others stay quiet.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6506.meaning: Deep meditation helps us understand how our physical body connects to our inner spiritual self.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6506.context: The text describes a deep spiritual truth about the body and the soul among great men.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6508.meaning: When we master our own mind and desires, our spirit can rise to a higher, peaceful place.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6508.context: A story describes a figure who controlled his self and then left his body to reach heaven.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6510.meaning: A life lived with peace and duty leads to a calm and happy transition after death.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6510.context: The king lives peacefully and finally joins the worlds of the ancestors after his life ends.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6512.meaning: Caring for those who have passed is a sacred duty that shows our deep love and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6512.context: The Pandavas and other relatives prepare wood and incense to build a funeral pyre for a loved one.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6513.meaning: We should treat our elders with great tenderness and care during their final moments of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6513.context: Family members dress in fine clothes and hold a woman gently as they prepare for her final rites.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6515.meaning: We show respect for our ancestors by creating a clean and beautiful space for their memory.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6515.context: The Kauravas are told to honor Bhishma by placing palm trees around his resting place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6516.meaning: Following ancient traditions shows deep respect for ancestors and helps maintain spiritual order in society.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6516.context: Priests performed sacred rituals for a great soul by offering gifts to the holy fire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6517.meaning: Using pure and pleasant items in worship reflects a sincere and devoted heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6517.context: They used sandalwood, blackberries, and fragrant spices like black pepper during the sacred ceremony.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6518.meaning: Following specific directions in rituals shows humility and obedience to divine laws.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6518.context: The ritual involved the Ganges river and fire while King Dhritarashtra and others turned left.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6519.meaning: Seeking the company of wise people helps us grow in knowledge and spiritual peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6519.context: The Kuru leaders reached the holy Ganges bank which was filled with many wise sages.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6520.meaning: Community unity in spiritual events strengthens social bonds and shared faith together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6520.context: Sages, Krishna, women, and all citizens followed the procession to the sacred river site.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6521.meaning: Participating in communal duties with care creates harmony and collective spiritual merit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6521.context: The warriors and people prepared water offerings for the Ganges following proper ritual rules.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6522.meaning: Devotion requires active effort and personal presence to achieve spiritual goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6522.context: Goddess Bhagirathi offered water to her son and then rose to approach the river.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6523.meaning: Sharing honest stories of the past helps others learn from mistakes and sins.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_13_6523.context: The Kauravas spoke sadly and asked listeners to hear the true story of past events.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_285.meaning: True leaders help others when they are lost. Kind words can heal a broken heart and bring peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_285.context: Krishna sees Arjuna is sad and confused. He speaks to comfort him and guide his troubled mind.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_286.meaning: Lying destroys your soul. Being honest connects you to God. Truth is the only path to real life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_286.context: The text contrasts lying with truth. It says deceit leads to death while honesty leads to divine life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_287.meaning: Your biggest problem is yourself. Fight your bad habits and pride. Conquer your inner self first.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_287.context: Arjuna has not finished his duty. He is told that his real enemy is his own ego.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_288.meaning: Learn from past stories. Righteous action is key. Use ancient wisdom to solve your modern problems today.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_288.context: Krishna promises to teach Arjuna the right way. He uses the story of Indra fighting Vritra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_289.meaning: Evil blocks the light. When truth is hidden, the world suffers. Darkness brings decay and pain to all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_289.context: Vritra covered the earth with darkness. The world suffered from decay and bad smells because of him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_290.meaning: Truth strikes hard against lies. Evil falls when justice arrives. Light always wins over darkness eventually.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_290.context: Indra struck Vritra with a lightning bolt. The demon fell down and the truth was revealed clearly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_292.meaning: Evil hides in small things. Do not let it grow. Strike it down quickly with strong will.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_292.context: Vritra tried to hide in taste. Indra got angry and threw another bolt to destroy the demon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_293.meaning: Darkness cannot survive in light. Truth clears everything up. Let brightness guide your actions always.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_293.context: Vritra was killed in the water. Light entered the scene and the matter was settled completely.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_431.meaning: King Dhritarashtra shows his respect for Kasyapa's intelligence and asks about the process of attaining liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_431.context: This verse is from the Hindu epic Mahabharata, where King Dhritarashtra addresses sage Kasyapa, expressing his admiration for his intelligence and seeking guidance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_432.meaning: King Dhritarashtra continues his discussion with Kasyapa, inquiring about the path to liberation from the material world.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_432.context: King Dhritarashtra continues his conversation with sage Kasyapa, discussing the process of achieving liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_435.meaning: Sage Sutikshna responds to King Dhritarashtra's inquiries, teaching him about the way to attain liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_435.context: Sage Sutikshna answers King Dhritarashtra's questions, guiding him towards understanding the path of liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_437.meaning: Sage Sutikshna emphasizes the significance of serving others without attachment to worldly things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_437.context: Sage Sutikshna explains the importance of serving others and being unattached to material possessions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_438.meaning: Sage Sutikshna highlights the significance of moderation in life's aspects like food, exercise, and desires to attain liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_438.context: Sage Sutikshna discusses the importance of moderation in food, exercise, and desires to achieve liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_440.meaning: Sage Sutikshna emphasizes the significance of detachment from material possessions and actions to achieve liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_440.context: Sage Sutikshna explains the importance of detachment from material possessions and actions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_441.meaning: Sage Sutikshna highlights the significance of self-control and detachment from desires, actions, and possessions to attain liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_441.context: Sage Sutikshna discusses the importance of self-control and detachment from desires, actions, and possessions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_442.meaning: Sage Sutikshna emphasizes the significance of self-control, detachment, and following the path of liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_442.context: Sage Sutikshna explains the importance of self-control, detachment, and the path of liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_711.meaning: Running away does not stop your inner pain. You must face your fears directly to find true peace and freedom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_711.context: People flee from others due to fear, feeling pain like a snake bite that never truly goes away.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_712.meaning: Your character defines your actions. Choose humility and kindness over pride to live a good and respected life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_712.context: Demons act arrogantly because of their nature, while gods give freely and wise sages stay humble and modest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_713.meaning: True wisdom can be simple. Listen carefully to wise teachers because their short advice can change your whole life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_713.context: Various beings including gods and demons went to a teacher and learned discipline from just one simple word.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_714.meaning: Stay humble and curious. Asking good questions shows respect and helps you learn deeper truths from those who know.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_714.context: A student listens carefully and accepts the truth. The more you ask questions, the more the teacher helps you.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_715.meaning: Your biggest obstacle is often your own ego. Listen to guidance to defeat the inner enemy that causes trouble.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_715.context: Actions follow permission. The teacher feels bound by duty, while the enemy of peace lives inside your own heart.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_716.meaning: Your habits shape who you are. Avoid bad actions because they will slowly turn you into a bad person.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_716.context: People who choose to walk in sin and bad behavior naturally become sinners and lose their good nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_717.meaning: Dedication to spiritual truth transforms you. When you focus on the divine, you become a vessel for higher wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_717.context: Those devoted to the sacred vow focus on the divine. In the spiritual world, you become a chariot of truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_719.meaning: God is in all things. See the sacred in nature and teachers to understand that everything is part of one whole.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_719.context: The divine is everywhere, in fire, water, and teachers. Everything is connected to the ultimate reality of Brahman.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_743.meaning: Simple living and deep focus help remove bad habits and bring you closer to the ultimate spiritual reality.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_743.context: Sages lived simply and burned away sins through strict discipline and deep meditation on the divine truth.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_744.meaning: Patience is a key virtue that makes a place or person worthy of respect and spiritual guidance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_744.context: Wise teachers praise this forest because it was born with great patience and serves as a holy place.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_745.meaning: Following wise guidance in sacred places helps you live correctly and gain deeper spiritual understanding.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_745.context: Brahmins know this forest is divine and they follow the expert instructions given for living there.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_746.meaning: True peace comes when you stop relying on your senses and find stillness within your own mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_746.context: The speaker describes a state where senses stop working and no physical forms or sounds are perceived.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_747.meaning: Uncontrolled desires act like fire, burning you up. You must control them to find true freedom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_747.context: The body is like fuel for desire, and violence feeds these animal instincts that keep us trapped.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_762.meaning: Simple truth is better than complex arguments. Trying too hard to explain God can ruin the real message.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_762.context: Understanding non-violence is complex, and trying to define the Supreme Being in many ways can confuse things.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_763.meaning: Being kind to all living things is the best form of worship and brings direct spiritual joy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_763.context: Non-violence pleases everyone and all beings. We practice it directly instead of worshipping through rituals.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_764.meaning: Appreciate the simple gifts of nature with your senses, finding joy in the world around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_764.context: Enjoy the earth's scent, water's taste, light's form, and air's touch as gifts from nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_773.meaning: The Brahmanas possess deep knowledge and understand a delicate path to liberation. They seek guidance from experienced individuals to navigate it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_773.context: In the Hindu epic Mahabharata, this verse describes the Brahmanas knowing a subtle form of liberation and following it under the guidance of experts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_774.meaning: Kartavirya Arjuna, a powerful warrior, talks to the sea, and the sea shows respect and seeks his help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_774.context: This verse narrates an ancient tale of Kartavirya Arjuna conversing with the sea.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_775.meaning: King Arjuna, having a thousand arms, shows his power near the sea, gaining admiration.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_775.context: Kartavirya Arjuna, a king with a thousand arms, demonstrates his strength near the sea.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_776.meaning: Arjuna, using his powerful arrows, instills fear in the sea, causing it to bow down and request help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_776.context: King Arjuna, with his mighty arrows, scares the sea and makes it bow down.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_777.meaning: Arjuna challenges others to engage in battle with him and desires to share the battlefield.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_777.context: King Arjuna challenges anyone to match his battle prowess and seek companionship.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_778.meaning: Arjuna advises King Partha to extend hospitality towards Jamadagni's son, showing respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_778.context: King Arjuna speaks to King Partha, suggesting hospitality towards Jamadagni's son.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_779.meaning: Arjuna, using his powerful arrows, showcases his strength near the sea, gaining admiration.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_779.context: King Arjuna, with his mighty arrows, demonstrates his strength near the sea.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_780.meaning: Arjuna, using his powerful arrows, instills fear in the sea, causing it to bow down and request help.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_780.context: King Arjuna, with his mighty arrows, scares the sea and makes it bow down.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1157.meaning: Understanding the impermanence of life and material possessions is essential. Just like a shadow and writing fade away, we should focus on inner peace and wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1157.context: In Hinduism, this verse from Mahabharata (Book 14:1157) discusses the transient nature of life and the impermanence of worldly pleasures.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1158.meaning: Our actions have consequences. Greed and desire lead to suffering, while love, wisdom, and detachment bring peace and happiness.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1158.context: Mahabharata (Book 14:1158) talks about the interconnectedness of cause and effect in Hinduism. The verse describes the consequences of greed and desire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1159.meaning: Life is a cycle of birth and death, with duality and conflict. To achieve peace, detach from worldly desires and focus on self-realization.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1159.context: The verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1161) highlights the duality of life and the importance of detachment in Hinduism.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1160.meaning: Life is temporary, and attachment causes suffering. By understanding and accepting this, one can achieve inner peace and liberation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1160.context: In Hinduism, verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1162) emphasizes the impermanence of life and the need to let go of attachment.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1161.meaning: Life is a journey towards liberation. By understanding the cycle of birth and death, one can break free from the cycle of suffering and attain spiritual growth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1161.context: This verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1163) discusses the cycle of birth and death in Hinduism, urging one to strive for liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1162.meaning: Detachment from worldly possessions and focusing on self-realization leads to inner peace and spiritual growth. Recognizing the impermanence of life helps in breaking free from suffering.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1162.context: In Hinduism, verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1164) highlights the importance of detachment and self-realization.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1163.meaning: Detachment from material possessions and focusing on self-realization brings inner peace and spiritual growth. Recognizing the impermanence of life helps in breaking free from suffering.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1163.context: This verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1165) emphasizes the importance of detachment and self-realization in Hinduism.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1164.meaning: Understanding the cycle of birth and death leads to liberation from suffering. By striving for liberation, one can achieve spiritual growth and inner peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1164.context: In Hinduism, verse (Mahabharata Book 14:1166) discusses the cycle of birth and death, urging one to strive for liberation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1496.meaning: Seeking peace, the soul asks to see the gentle and loving side of the divine creator once more.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1496.context: Arjuna asks Krishna to show his divine universal form again after seeing the terrifying vision of destruction.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1497.meaning: It is wise to offer simple and pure gifts rather than complex or inappropriate ones to others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1497.context: A sage advises against giving a strange gift and suggests offering water from a sacred source instead.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1512.meaning: Sometimes wise leaders stay quiet to teach a lesson about patience and accepting difficult truths calmly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1512.context: Krishna remains silent and does not comfort the sage Uttanka with soft words after his request is denied.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1513.meaning: We often miss the value of good gifts because we lack the wisdom to see their worth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1513.context: The speaker explains that the gift offered was worthy but the recipient failed to understand its true value.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1514.meaning: Divine grace can transform ordinary things into sacred blessings for those who are worthy and faithful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1514.context: The Lord commands that nectar be given as water to Uttanka for the sake of the god Indra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1515.meaning: When leaders ask for help with humility, the divine source is willing to provide what is needed.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1515.context: The speaker recounts how Indra asked for nectar and the Lord agreed to provide it to him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1517.meaning: We must consider the consequences of our actions before giving, as some gifts change us forever.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1517.context: The speaker warns that giving the gift will turn him into an elephant, so he gives it to Bhrigu.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1518.meaning: If you refuse a blessing when it is offered, you may lose the chance to receive it later.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1518.context: The speaker declares he will give the nectar to others since Bhrigu rejected the offer previously made.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1753.meaning: Listen to wise leaders, accept their choices, and do not dwell on past decisions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1753.context: Krishna, a heroic hero, speaks to the Kurus about a decision that has already been made.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1764.meaning: Follow wise counsel, do what is right, and keep your promises to others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1764.context: Bhishma and Govinda advise the Pandavas to act correctly and remember their duties.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1765.meaning: Recognize scarcity, share resources, and value what is truly precious in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1765.context: The Kurus discuss the earth's lack of precious stones and show the wealth of Marutta.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1767.meaning: Seek group wisdom, consider all views, and choose the best path together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1767.context: People debate whether a decision is correct or wrong and ask for collective input.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1768.meaning: Show respect, speak honestly, and honor the leaders who guide you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1768.context: Two kings speak with respect, and Bhimasena gives a heartfelt reply to the leaders.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1769.meaning: Celebrate generosity, value shared resources, and honor those who give freely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1769.context: A mighty warrior praises another for sharing the wealth of a certain age or era.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1770.meaning: Trust in effort, believe in success, and keep working toward your goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1770.context: Someone promises to find money and believes it will be completed soon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1771.meaning: Seek blessings, honor nature, and pray for prosperity and protection.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1771.context: They call upon a mountain lord to bring blessings and worship for good fortune.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1802.meaning: He learns that many things can be useful, and he must decide how to use them wisely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1802.context: Yudhisthira, a righteous king, sees many different kinds of vessels.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1803.meaning: He understands that many options exist, and he should choose the best ones for his people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1803.context: Yudhisthira, the king, notices many thousands of various vessels.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1806.meaning: He sees that many tools can aid in good work, and he should use them carefully.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1806.context: Yudhisthira sees many different types of vessels to help him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1808.meaning: He learns that many resources are available, and he must use them responsibly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1808.context: Yudhisthira, the king, observes many thousands of various vessels.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1809.meaning: He realizes that many options exist, and he should choose the right ones for his tasks.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1809.context: Yudhisthira sees many kinds of vessels ready for use.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1811.meaning: He sees that many tools are available, and he must use them wisely for good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1811.context: Yudhisthira, the king, notes many thousands of various vessels.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1812.meaning: He learns that great resources can be shared, but must be managed carefully.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1812.context: The king hears about large bags and many vessels holding many items.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1813.meaning: He sees that many powerful tools exist, and he should use them for the benefit of all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1813.context: The king is told about many elephants, carts, and chariots, hard to count.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1916.meaning: Good actions earn praise from higher powers, showing that doing right brings recognition.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1916.context: Demons left Neshu, a voice praised Keshav for his good deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1917.meaning: Sacrifice and courage can restore life and inspire joy in those who witness it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1917.context: Grandfather left with a burning weapon, father regained life, child moved excitedly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1918.meaning: Learning sacred texts strengthens faith, while recognizing that even rulers face challenges from evil.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1918.context: King Bharata and satriyas celebrated, reading Brahmanas, demons ruled by Govinda.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1919.meaning: Praise for strength shows that skill and bravery are valued, even in difficult situations.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1919.context: All praised Janardana, satyrs skilled, like finding a lion boat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1920.meaning: Unity among people, even those seen as fierce, brings joy and shared celebration.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1920.context: Kunti, Subhadra, and others among lions celebrated together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1921.meaning: Timely action and welcoming others lead to blessings and generosity from those around.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1921.context: Rise early, go north, Yadus welcomed a fairy and her son, gifts given.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1923.meaning: Honoring promises builds trust, and being called noble shows respect from the community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1923.context: Others named him Vrishnishardula, king praised for keeping promises.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1932.meaning: Even in secrecy, leaders must manage many people, showing the complexity of leadership.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_14_1932.context: King had many people, prisoners, decorated places hidden from view.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_50.meaning: Bad people often cause pain and hatred among wise folks. You should stay away from such toxic individuals in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_50.context: A wise speaker warns the queen about a man who brings trouble and anger to those around him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_52.meaning: Fear stops people from admitting mistakes. You must be brave enough to fix your errors and do what is right.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_52.context: The speaker notes that the blind king and his son did not correct their wrong actions or bad behavior.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_53.meaning: Stay calm and pure even when facing enemies. Your good character matters more than the bad actions of others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_53.context: The queen and wise minister liked the king's calm patience. The enemy was born from pure actions, not hate.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_54.meaning: Feel compassion for those who suffer. Even strong warriors should show kindness and sorrow for others pain.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_54.context: Bhima followed the good king closely. He felt deep sadness when looking at the blind king Dhritarashtra.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_55.meaning: True loyalty comes from the heart. Do not just follow others if your mind is full of anger and hate.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_55.context: The wise son followed the king with respect. The Kauravas followed but their hearts were turned away in hate.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_56.meaning: Love for family can blind us. Try to see things clearly without letting personal feelings cloud your judgment.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_56.context: The king thought about his young son. He could not focus on Bhima because his mind was clouded by love.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_58.meaning: Do not hide your true feelings. It is better to be honest than to fake happiness while holding onto anger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_58.context: Bhima spoke to the king respectfully. He asked the ruler not to stay angry or pretend to be happy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_59.meaning: Do not betray those who help you. Being ungrateful and disobedient leads to trouble and breaks trust with others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_59.context: The wolf did bad things to him. He always disobeyed the orders of the men who had helped him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_144.meaning: Listening to good counsel saves a ruler from pointless death and keeps his reign meaningful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_144.context: A king is warned that if he ignores wise advice, he will die without purpose.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_145.meaning: True leadership comes from learning ancient teachings and living simply, like sages in nature.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_145.context: The king is urged to follow ancient sages who seek refuge in forests for wisdom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_147.meaning: Recognizing God as teacher and king reminds us to respect divine guidance in all life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_147.context: The verse praises God as a respected teacher and the supreme ruler of the kingdom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_148.meaning: Family roles and duty are linked, showing respect for elders and leaders in everyday life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_148.context: The speaker identifies with son, father, king, and teacher, showing deep family and duty ties.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_150.meaning: Seeking permission from higher powers helps avoid chaos and keeps intentions clear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_150.context: The speaker asks the earth’s lord to allow their plans, warning of possible disruptions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_152.meaning: Sacred practices guide warriors, and death in battle or nature is seen as a noble end.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_152.context: The verse describes the royal sages’ main religion and the fate of those who die in battle or forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_153.meaning: Even rulers learn from nature and respect their leaders, showing humility and devotion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_153.context: The king’s father, Pandu, looks to the earth, becomes a disciple, and worships the king as teacher.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_154.meaning: Sharing food and support builds community, showing love and generosity toward family and friends.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_154.context: People decorate a mountain with food, supported by great ones who love and enjoy them with their sons.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_487.meaning: Even kings seek divine presence; the Lord appears where devotion and humility meet.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_487.context: Dhritarashtra traveled far, and the Lord settled beside the Bhagi Rathi river.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_488.meaning: True power comes from knowledge, discipline, and honoring sacred traditions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_488.context: Fire worshipers, skilled in Vedas, ruled with celestial power and austerity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_489.meaning: Sacred acts bring clarity and illumination to the heart and mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_489.context: The king offered fire rituals, and evening light revealed many bright rays.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_490.meaning: Respectful care for leaders shows humility and strengthens communal bonds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_490.context: Vidura and Sanjayasha prepared the king’s bed with kusha grass near Gandhari.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_491.meaning: Steadfast devotion inspires others to follow righteous paths.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_491.context: He sat near Gandhari; Kunti, Yudhisthira’s mother, upheld her vows.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_492.meaning: Listening to wise guidance helps maintain harmony and spiritual growth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_492.context: Vavidura and others listened to priests, gods, and followers following instructions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_493.meaning: Even in loss, light can guide and uplift the spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_493.context: The fire was lit by defeated Davijas, bringing night like Brahma’s light.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_494.meaning: Shared sorrow unites communities and reminds us of compassion.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_494.context: They endured a sad first day; townspeople mourned deeply.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1051.meaning: Respecting rituals shows humility and gratitude, reminding us to honor customs and share generosity with others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1051.context: On the twelfth day, the king was cleansed, and the Pandavas gave alms as tradition requires.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1052.meaning: Material riches can be abundant, but true value lies in how we use them to help and uplift people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1052.context: The earth’s ruler gave Dhritarashtra wealth, gold, silver, cows, and comfortable bedding.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1053.meaning: Uncontrolled desire leads to endless wants, teaching that contentment brings peace rather than endless consumption.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1053.context: A man who wants everything gets beds, food, cars, gems, and wealth without limits.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1055.meaning: Offering gifts shows respect, but true honor comes from sincere service and genuine care for others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1055.context: The carriage, cover, food, maids, and attendants were given to the king to honor him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1056.meaning: Preparedness and wisdom help navigate challenges, reminding us to stay ready and seek knowledge in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1056.context: The earth’s king gave many arrows, and a wise man returned to Varanasi again.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1057.meaning: Duty can pull us away from loved ones, yet balance and reflection help maintain family bonds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1057.context: Men went to the palace at the king’s command, left families, and returned after deciding to leave.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1058.meaning: Rituals unite people, showing that shared faith and communication strengthen community and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1058.context: They worshiped him with garlands and oils, gathered families, and informed the king as tradition dictates.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1059.meaning: Seeking wise counsel brings clarity, encouraging us to listen to experienced voices during difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_15_1059.context: After comforting Yudhisthira, Narada came to the king, as the great sage requested.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_638.meaning: True leadership shines brightly for everyone to see and guides people through darkness with clear and steady light.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_638.context: The text describes a powerful ruler whose influence spreads widely across the land like bright sunlight.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_639.meaning: Pride and aggression lead to ruin. Those who attack with arrogance will destroy themselves just like bugs in flames.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_639.context: Kings arrive with large armies but face destruction because they act like insects flying directly into fire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_640.meaning: Accepting shared rules and duties brings harmony. Just as rivers accept rain, leaders should embrace common laws.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_640.context: The ruler accepts the laws and duties set by other kings, flowing naturally like river water meets rain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_641.meaning: A good leader protects everyone equally. Fairness allows society to grow and thrive like healthy crops in soil.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_641.context: He holds the four social groups together properly, making the earth fair and good for all crops.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_642.meaning: True authority is natural and universal. Like the wind, a wise leader connects with and guides all people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_642.context: All kings obey his command because he is like the wind that moves through all living beings.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_643.meaning: Divine power is vast and unstoppable. It reminds us that ultimate strength belongs to the divine forces of nature.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_643.context: Rudra the destroyer appears strong in all worlds, showing power that reaches even the ends of the sea.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_644.meaning: Sometimes we must record events as they happen. Accepting the past allows us to move forward with peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_644.context: The sage writes down the story without focusing on causes, recording the release of King Brihadratha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_645.meaning: Transitioning power with family support brings peace. Helping others find relief creates stability and harmony for all.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_645.context: He enters the city with family support and crowns Jarasandha, bringing relief and peace to the old king.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_674.meaning: We should act with care to calm down angry people and stop them from causing harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_674.context: The heroes dressed in special clothes to calm the angry people who were causing trouble.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_675.meaning: True strength comes from staying focused and united with your partner when facing a tough enemy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_675.context: Bhima saw Jarasandh and thought he was dead, but the two Krishnas stayed strong in battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_676.meaning: Great leaders help us start good work and control our desires to live a righteous life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_676.context: The two great lords guide all actions, including how we handle wealth, desire, and duty.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_677.meaning: Life is a journey where we must keep moving forward through different places and challenges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_677.context: The group moved past the Kuru lands into the forest and headed toward a beautiful lake area.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_678.meaning: Nature has a strong power that we should respect and admire in our daily lives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_678.context: The blue rivers flow down the mountains with great force, showing the power of nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_679.meaning: We must keep moving through different stages of life to reach our final destination.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_679.context: They crossed the Sarayu river and traveled through Mithila to reach a place with many rivers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_680.meaning: Sometimes we must leave familiar places behind to move toward a new and important goal.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_680.context: After crossing the Ganges and Shona rivers, the group turned away and headed to Magadha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_681.meaning: Good things often come to those who keep moving forward with a positive and hopeful heart.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_681.context: The water was fragrant and lucky, and they reached a mountain and saw the city of Magadha.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_996.meaning: True wisdom sees past words to the heart. We should trust deep understanding over surface appearances.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_996.context: Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up because he knows the true thoughts of everyone present.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_997.meaning: Loyalty to duty and personal choice can coexist. We should honor our promises while respecting others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_997.context: A warrior promises to defend the city while the rightful king lives, but follows Arjuna's wishes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_998.meaning: Joy comes from sincere devotion. We find peace when we offer our hearts to something greater.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_998.context: A brave man stands up happily and bows his hands to worship the sacred fire altar.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_999.meaning: Respect is shown through humble actions. We honor strength by approaching it with a gentle spirit.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_999.context: After the fire goes out, a blue king walks respectfully toward the mighty warrior Sahadeva.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1000.meaning: Action follows intention. We must be ready to move quickly when the time for success arrives.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1000.context: The warrior takes back the worship item and runs away south to win a great victory.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1001.meaning: Strength brings responsibility. True power is used to protect people and establish order in the land.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1001.context: A hero conquers a city and becomes a powerful king with arms of great strength.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1002.meaning: History teaches us about courage. We learn from past heroes how to face difficult challenges bravely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1002.context: A speaker recalls how he brought a teacher and how Rama defeated a local king.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1003.meaning: Communication bridges different levels of power. We must speak clearly to connect with those in charge.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_1003.context: A subject is sent to a king named Rukmi who is sitting in a grand banquet hall.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2207.meaning: Power is temporary and changes hands. Do not cling to authority because it will eventually pass to someone else.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2207.context: The speaker reflects on how power shifts between families over time like waves in the ocean.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2208.meaning: Take responsibility for your role. Stand up for what is right and lead your people with courage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2208.context: A character urges Yudhisthira to take action and reclaim his rightful place among the people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2209.meaning: Do not let fear dictate your actions. Use your intellect to make fair decisions instead of reacting in panic.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2209.context: The assembly members argue that fear should not control wise leaders who understand true justice.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2210.meaning: Listen to what others say. Understanding public opinion helps leaders make better choices for their community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2210.context: The narrator invites the king to listen to the stories and rumors circulating among the people.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2211.meaning: Bad habits can destroy families. Be aware of your actions and avoid risks that harm your loved ones.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2211.context: The wise man returns to gambling without realizing the danger it poses to his family.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2212.meaning: Doing the right thing is hard. Stay true to your values even when others pressure you to compromise.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2212.context: Yudhisthira questions how he can remain righteous when faced with difficult choices and pressure.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2213.meaning: Accept your fate with grace. Facing hardship together with family makes the burden easier to bear.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2213.context: The brothers accept their exile and decide to live in the forest together.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2215.meaning: Sometimes stepping back is wise. Living simply in nature can help you keep your integrity intact.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2215.context: The speaker suggests living in the forest as a way to maintain their honor.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2252.meaning: Leadership should be shared, respecting others, to keep peace and fairness in society.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2252.context: A king must share his rule after fourteen years, honoring Duryodhana.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2253.meaning: Listening to wise teachers and uniting with brave friends strengthens courage and wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2253.context: Vaishampayana speaks to Partha, then Sahadeva, a brave warrior, gathers others.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2254.meaning: Pride can be mistaken; true power comes from humility and genuine skill.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2254.context: Someone mocks the Gandharvas, claiming their glory is weak and unsharp.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2256.meaning: True friends act for others, showing loyalty and support in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2256.context: Bhima tells relatives he will act for them, doing their deeds.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2257.meaning: Stand firm for justice, but remember compassion and fairness guide true strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2257.context: A warrior vows to kill enemies, urging them to fight for righteousness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2258.meaning: Words can hurt; choose kindness and respect to avoid conflict and harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2258.context: A woman of Yajnasena speaks sharply to Duryodhana, warning him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2260.meaning: Wrong actions bring suffering; learning from mistakes helps prevent future harm.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2260.context: They die because of Dhritarashtra’s bad deeds; a great destruction is shown.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2261.meaning: Following wise leaders can create a stable, united community for everyone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_2_2261.context: A king follows Daraupadya’s path, promising to build a strong nation soon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4.meaning: True strength comes from keeping your word, even when it means living in hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_4.context: Great heroes spent twelve years hiding in a forest to keep a promise.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6.meaning: Honesty and loyalty are true virtues, even when you suffer for them without fault.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6.context: A noble princess stayed loyal to her family during their unfair exile.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_7.meaning: We should always seek the full truth to understand people and events clearly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_7.context: A king asks a wise man to tell the full story of a hero.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8.meaning: Bad leaders and their followers often cause great harm and destruction to others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8.context: Angry enemies were defeated by a wicked king and his bad advisors.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9.meaning: Sometimes you must leave your home and face danger to do what is right.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9.context: A group of warriors left a city gate with weapons to go north.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_10.meaning: Loyal friends will stand by you and protect you when you are in danger.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_10.context: Fourteen loyal servants followed their leader in chariots to protect a prince.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_11.meaning: Wise people can help calm fear and sadness by speaking with care and reason.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_11.context: Citizens were sad about a wedding, and wise elders spoke to calm them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_12.meaning: Greed for power brings deep sadness and breaks the peace of a whole family.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_12.context: People felt sorrow because a greedy man wanted the throne and caused pain.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_43.meaning: Seek wise counsel from learned individuals, even when they appear differently. Trust and help those in need.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_43.context: The wise brahmins, disguised as swans, approached the king for protection and guidance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_44.meaning: Simplicity and humility lead to inner peace. Support those in misfortune.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_44.context: King Yudhisthira and his brothers decided to live a simple life in the forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_45.meaning: Understanding others' circumstances and empathizing helps gods and humans alike.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_45.context: The brahmins mentioned the dangers and hardships of living in the forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_46.meaning: Show compassion to those in need, as gods and humans can benefit from it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_46.context: King Yudhisthira reassured the brahmins of their safety and well-being.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_47.meaning: Trust in the wisdom of righteous leaders and support their decisions.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_47.context: The brahmins pledged to follow King Yudhisthira's guidance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_48.meaning: Respect and help those devoted to the divine, as they are blessed.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_48.context: King Yudhisthira addressed the brahmins' suffering and devotion.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_49.meaning: Accept help from righteous individuals and trust in their wisdom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_49.context: The brahmins accepted King Yudhisthira's offer of protection and guidance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_50.meaning: Assure and care for those in need, as it brings blessings.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_50.context: King Yudhisthira assured the brahmins of their safety.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_852.meaning: Visiting holy places with good people helps you feel closer to the divine and find peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_852.context: The king and his group travel to the Pandavas home in a sacred forest.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_854.meaning: Nature shows us God's beauty, reminding us to appreciate the world around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_854.context: The king sees a beautiful forest full of blooming trees and flowers in summer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_855.meaning: Listening to nature's sounds can calm your mind and bring you inner joy.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_855.context: Birds sing sweetly from high trees while the king watches the lively forest scene.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_856.meaning: All living beings are part of God's creation and deserve our respect and care.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_856.context: The king observes large groups of ducks and other animals living freely in the woods.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_857.meaning: True strength comes from living simply and focusing on spiritual growth, not material things.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_857.context: The king sees holy men living simply in the forest, wearing matted hair and bark.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_858.meaning: Humility means leaving behind your status to connect deeply with others and nature.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_858.context: The king leaves his chariot and walks into the forest with his family members.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_859.meaning: Being mindful and present allows you to truly see and understand the people around you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_859.context: Forest dwellers and holy men stand around the king, watching him with focused attention.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_860.meaning: Respect and kindness build strong bonds, showing that everyone has inherent worth and dignity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_860.context: The king greets the holy men, who honor him as a king and a god.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1005.meaning: When you let anger take over, you may hurt others and ruin your own life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1005.context: A very angry man starts fighting and ends up killing many people around him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1006.meaning: Anger can break the strongest family bonds and lead to terrible violence between loved ones.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1006.context: The text describes a time when family members turn against each other and cause great harm.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1007.meaning: Holding onto anger is dangerous because it can destroy everyone around you, including yourself.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1007.context: The story warns that unchecked anger can lead to the total destruction of a whole community.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1009.meaning: Life is full of strange changes, and we must accept that things do not always go as planned.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1009.context: The text reflects on how life and death seem to happen in a confusing and reversed way.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1012.meaning: Small bad thoughts can grow big and destroy your peace, so you must watch your mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1012.context: The verse talks about how small, angry thoughts can ruin a person's future happiness and peace.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1013.meaning: True strength comes from forgiving others, just like the wise leaders of old did.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1013.context: Great sages and wise leaders are remembered for their ability to forgive others who hurt them.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1014.meaning: Wise and holy people show their goodness by forgiving others instead of holding grudges.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1014.context: People who know the truth and live simply are also known for being very forgiving.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_1017.meaning: Forgiving others is a noble act that brings peace and helps you enjoy a better life later.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5193.context: A fierce demon prepares for a violent fight, charging forward with the speed and power of a lightning strike.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5203.meaning: War causes deep harm to the earth and innocent life. We must seek peace to protect our shared home and community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5203.context: The battle destroys the natural environment, cutting down trees and ruining the land as warriors fight to kill each other.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5204.meaning: Conflict creates chaos that affects everyone around it. We should avoid arguments that destroy stability and bring fear to others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5204.context: Stones fly through the air like heavy clouds colliding, showing the intense and chaotic nature of the ongoing battle.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5205.meaning: Anger makes people act quickly and violently. We must control our temper to avoid causing unnecessary pain and damage.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5205.context: The fighters look fierce and move with great speed, striking their opponents with the force of powerful thunderbolts.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5206.meaning: Justice sometimes requires strong action against wrongdoers. However, we should always aim to stop harm rather than enjoy it.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5206.context: The Pandavas attack the enemy, crushing his limbs and causing him great physical pain during the intense combat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5207.meaning: Swift and decisive action can stop evil. We should act bravely and quickly when we see injustice happening around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5207.context: Bhima fights with the speed of a serpent, striking the demon's head quickly to end the dangerous confrontation.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5208.meaning: Standing up for truth may be hard. But protecting the weak from bullies is a duty we must fulfill with strength.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5208.context: The heroes continue to overpower the enemy, breaking his body parts as the fight reaches its critical and painful stage.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5210.meaning: Evil eventually falls when faced with courage. The victory of good brings safety and peace to the suffering people.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_5210.context: Bhima holds the demon's bloody head, showing the final defeat of the enemy who caused much trouble and fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6329.meaning: True wisdom and inner light make a person stand out and inspire others around them.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6329.context: Paratapavan was a wise sage who shone brightly like a god among men.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6330.meaning: Hard work and dedication allow you to achieve more than those who came before you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6330.context: Manu and his ancestors surpassed their father through great energy, luxury, and strict self discipline.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6331.meaning: Deep focus and physical discipline help you connect with the divine and find inner peace.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6331.context: The king stood on one foot in a tree with arms raised for deep prayer.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6332.meaning: Patience and steady focus over long periods lead to great spiritual strength and clarity.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6332.context: He kept his head down and eyes steady while meditating for many thousands of years.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6333.meaning: Even the smallest creatures need protection from stronger ones, so we must help the weak.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6333.context: A small fish begged the king to save it from bigger fish that eat it.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6335.meaning: Nature is harsh, but we should not ignore the suffering of those weaker than us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6335.context: The fish explained that bigger fish naturally eat smaller ones as part of their custom.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6336.meaning: When we are in deep trouble, we must ask for help from those who can save us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6336.context: The fish said it was drowning in fear and deserved to be saved by the king.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6337.meaning: Compassion moves us to act kindly and protect those who are vulnerable and afraid.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_6337.context: Manu felt deep compassion for the fish and gently picked it up with his hand.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8964.meaning: Guilt can destroy us when we realize we have lied to someone who deserves our respect and trust.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8964.context: The deer sees Rama and feels deep shame for tricking the holy man with his disguise.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8965.meaning: Knowing the truth about our wrong actions brings heavy shame that can lead to our downfall quickly.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8965.context: The deer realizes he is facing Rama and feels overwhelmed by shame before dying from the arrow.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8966.meaning: Evil often uses familiar voices to trick loved ones into making dangerous choices that hurt them deeply.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8966.context: The dying deer cries out in Rama's voice to trick Sita and Lakshmana into leaving their safe spot.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8967.meaning: Emotional reactions can blind us to danger when we ignore wise advice from those who care.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8967.context: Sita hears the fake cry and runs toward the sound despite Lakshmana trying to stop her from going.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8968.meaning: Trust in your loved ones and stay calm because fear often makes us see problems that are not real.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8968.context: Lakshmana tells Sita to stop doubting and assures her that Rama will return to them very soon.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8969.meaning: Deep love makes us value our partner more than our own life and safety in difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8969.context: Sita declares she would rather die by fire or fall from a mountain than live without her husband.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8972.meaning: Loyalty to one person means rejecting others and choosing a hard path rather than breaking your vows.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8972.context: Sita says she is not Lakshmana's wife and will leave to live alone in the wild like a beast.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8973.meaning: True devotion brings joy to those who love you and gives them strength to face their enemies bravely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_8973.context: Rama and Lakshmana are pleased with Sita's loyalty and follow the deer's tracks to find the enemy.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9082.meaning: Trust the words of those who speak with care, as they may bring comfort and guidance in hard times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9082.context: A horse speaks to Sita in the forest, asking her to listen carefully to his important message.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9083.meaning: Even unlikely sources can bring good news, showing that help can come from unexpected places in life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9083.context: The horse mentions a demon chief who wants to help Rama and shares news for Sita's benefit.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9084.meaning: Knowing your loved ones are safe brings peace to your heart and reduces worry during difficult moments.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9084.context: The horse tells Sita that her husband Rama is safe and strong with his brother Lakshmana.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9085.meaning: Building strong alliances and doing your best work helps you overcome obstacles and achieve your goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9085.context: Rama has made friends with the monkey king and is preparing to rescue Sita from her captivity.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9086.meaning: Past mistakes and curses do not define your future, as you can still choose to do good.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9086.context: The horse describes a past failure involving a woman named Rambha and his own cursed nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9087.meaning: Hope remains strong when you know that loyal friends are working hard to bring you relief soon.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9087.context: The horse promises that Rama and his allies will soon arrive to free Sita from her troubles.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9089.meaning: Bad feelings or dreams can sometimes signal that justice is coming for those who do evil deeds.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9089.context: The horse shares bad dreams he had, which predict the downfall of the wicked demon Ravana.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9090.meaning: Do not judge others by their appearance, as even those who seem scary can offer kindness and truth.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9090.context: The horse admits he is a scary creature by nature but is speaking truth to help Sita now.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9091.meaning: When your time is done, you cannot stop fate. Accept that all power fades and endings are natural parts of life.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9091.context: A dream shows a powerful figure whose time has come to end his reign and face defeat.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9092.meaning: Pride leads to humiliation. Those who act arrogantly will eventually be laughed at and lose their dignity and respect.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9092.context: A ten faced king is mocked in a dream, riding a donkey and covered in mud and oil.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9093.meaning: Loss of power leaves you vulnerable. When strength fades, you may face shame and struggle with heavy burdens alone.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9093.context: Warriors appear naked and weak in a vision, losing their strength and pulling heavy burdens in shame.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9095.meaning: Purity brings peace. By staying clean in heart and mind, you can overcome great fears and find true freedom.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9095.context: Secretaries wear white garlands in a dream, symbolizing purity and the promise of freedom from fear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9096.meaning: Great actions leave lasting marks. Your deeds can change the world and bring you honor that lasts forever.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9096.context: A weapon shatters the earth and sea, while a husband gains fame that fills the entire world.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9097.meaning: Stay alert and enjoy life. Even in strange times, keep your eyes open and trust those who watch over you.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9097.context: A dreamer rides on bones and eats sweet food, while a loyal brother watches carefully in all directions.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9098.meaning: Protection comes in hard times. Even when you suffer greatly, unexpected help may guard you through your darkest moments.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9098.context: A woman cries with blood on her body, yet a young tiger protects her as she travels north.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9099.meaning: Hope remains in sorrow. Even in deep sadness, believe that joy and reunion with loved ones are coming soon.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9099.context: A prophecy tells a crying woman that she will soon rejoice and be reunited with her beloved husband.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9100.meaning: Even in deep sadness, outside forces can intrude, showing that life keeps moving around us.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9100.context: A woman sits sadly with messy hair while terrible vampires arrive to disturb her peace.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9102.meaning: Grief can make us feel unworthy, yet our true value remains unchanged by our outer appearance.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9102.context: A grieving woman wears dirty clothes but is also shown with jewels, highlighting her mixed state.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9103.meaning: Lust can blind us to proper respect, driving us to act on selfish wants instead of honor.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9103.context: A demon king sees a woman being worshiped by others and feels strong desire to approach her.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9104.meaning: Uncontrolled desire can defeat even the strongest people, leading them away from their true path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9104.context: A warrior fights many beings but ends up lost in a forest because of strong desire.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9105.meaning: Beauty and grace can be powerful, but they are often just the surface of a deeper story.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9105.context: A handsome man wears divine clothes and beautiful jewelry, looking like a sculpture of spring.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9106.meaning: People can seem wonderful on the outside while hiding dark or dangerous truths within.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9106.context: A man is compared to a wish-fulfilling tree but also looks like a scary cemetery tree.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9107.meaning: We often observe others from a distance, feeling small or hidden when facing someone powerful.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9107.context: A man watches a woman approaching, comparing her to a planet and himself to a night owl.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9108.meaning: Words and charm can be used to influence others, so we must listen carefully to intent.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9108.context: A man invites a woman and uses his charm, speaking to a child who is very strong.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9200.meaning: Leaders must listen to their people and gather together to solve big problems.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9200.context: Rama sits with his army while Sugriva calls all the monkey chiefs to gather.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9201.meaning: True friends show up with their full support when you need help the most.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9201.context: Sushena, a noble monkey chief, comes to Rama with a huge group of monkeys.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9202.meaning: Sometimes you must split up to cover more ground and find all your allies.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9203.meaning: Even the strangest or scariest people can be part of your team if they are loyal.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9203.context: A scary round-tailed monkey named Gavaksha appears with many other strange and wild animals.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9204.meaning: Your circle of support can grow much bigger than you ever imagined at first.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9204.context: A monkey from a high mountain brings a massive group of fierce deer to the camp.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9205.meaning: Bringing your full strength and energy to the group helps everyone succeed together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9205.context: A green warrior named Dadhimukha arrives with a large and bright army of monkeys.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9206.meaning: Experience and wisdom are valuable assets that can guide a team to victory.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9206.context: An older green warrior named Dadhimukh brings a huge army of shining monkeys to help.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9207.meaning: Strength comes from unity, and even the mightiest individuals need a strong community.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9207.context: Jambavan, a powerful bear, appears with a massive crowd of his own followers.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9394.meaning: True wisdom can bind even strong enemies, showing that knowledge is a mighty force in battle.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9394.context: Vibhishana arrives to help the heroes who are trapped by a powerful weapon of knowledge.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9395.meaning: Healing often comes from nature and faith, reminding us to seek help from both sources.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9395.context: Sugriva uses special herbs and holy chants to help the two heroes recover their strength quickly.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9396.meaning: When you overcome a hard trial, the obstacles vanish, and you stand ready for the next step.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9396.context: The two men wake up feeling fresh and strong, and the dangerous traps around them disappear.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9397.meaning: Showing respect to a leader builds trust and unity among friends during difficult times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9397.context: Vibhishana sees Rama is healthy again and speaks to him respectfully with his hands folded.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9398.meaning: Sometimes we need special help to see the truth that is hidden from our normal view.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9398.context: Vibhishana explains that the king ordered this water to be given to reveal hidden secrets.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9399.meaning: Divine gifts can open our eyes to see the truth and protect us from unseen dangers.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9399.context: The water is a gift from Kubera, meant to help Rama see things that are not visible.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9400.meaning: Accepting help with gratitude and using it wisely shows strength and respect for the giver.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9400.context: Rama accepts the water with honor, and Lakshmana uses it to clean his eyes carefully.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9402.meaning: Having a strong group of loyal friends makes you feel safe and ready for any challenge.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9402.context: The text lists the best warriors and friends who are ready to support the main heroes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9688.meaning: Following the teachings of righteous people and dedicating oneself to the religion of Dharma leads to a fulfilling life. Emphasizing the importance of righteousness.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9689.meaning: Trusting in one's partner and following their advice ensures safety and protection.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9689.context: The story of Chayuta, who sought refuge with her husband and followed his guidance.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9690.meaning: Being virtuous and compatible with others brings happiness and harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9690.context: The virtue of being virtuous and compatible with others is praised.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9691.meaning: Seeking wisdom and guidance from wise people leads to personal growth and enlightenment.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9692.meaning: Wise elders play a crucial role in guiding and protecting their family.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9693.meaning: Sacrificing worldly possessions for the well-being of family brings peace and harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9693.context: The story of Chayuta's father-in-law, who chose to leave his kingdom for the sake of his family.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9694.meaning: Putting family first and prioritizing their well-being is commendable.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9694.context: The story of Chayuta's father-in-law, who chose to leave his kingdom for the sake of his family.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9695.meaning: Sacrificing personal interests for the well-being of family brings happiness and harmony.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9695.context: The story of Chayuta's father-in-law, who chose to leave his kingdom for the sake of his family.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9652.meaning: True love means being ready to suffer and stay strong without complaining or asking for any special treatment from others.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9652.context: Savitri speaks to her father-in-law about her deep devotion and willingness to endure hardship for her husband.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9653.meaning: When you seek permission, promise to act with care and respect so that no harm comes to your reputation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9653.context: She asks her guru to allow her to follow her husband, promising to behave well and avoid mistakes.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9654.meaning: Honesty about difficult plans helps family members understand the situation and prepare for the changes ahead together.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9654.context: Savitri tells her father-in-law that her husband is going to the forest to live a simple life.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9655.meaning: Staying close to loved ones during tough times shows deep care and helps both people feel less lonely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9655.context: She explains that being apart from her husband is hard, so she wants to go with him.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9656.meaning: Understanding the purpose behind someone's actions helps us accept their choices even when they seem difficult or distant.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9656.context: She reminds him that her husband is doing a sacred duty, and the forest is far away.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9657.meaning: It is natural to want new experiences after a long time of routine, but always keep your duties in mind.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9657.context: Savitri says she has stayed in the ashram for a year and now wants to see nature.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9658.meaning: Respecting family bonds and past promises helps resolve conflicts and brings peace to everyone involved in the situation.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9658.context: The father-in-law accepts her request because she was given to him by his own father.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9659.meaning: Freedom comes with responsibility, so always choose honesty and good behavior even when no one is watching you closely.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9659.context: He grants her wish but warns her to stay on the path of truth while traveling.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9634.meaning: True love means making great sacrifices for others, even when the situation seems hopeless or very difficult.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9634.context: Savitri fasted for days to save her husband from death, showing deep love and devotion.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9643.meaning: When you act with pure intentions, wise people recognize your goodness and support your noble goals.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9643.context: Holy men in the forest praised Savitri, saying her actions were good and brought blessings to all.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9645.meaning: Patience and reflection help us stay calm and focused when we face difficult or sad times.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9645.context: The princess waited sadly for the right moment, remembering the wise words of the sage Narada.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9646.meaning: Elders often share important advice to guide us through tough choices and help us understand our path.
hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9646.context: Her father-in-law spoke to her, sharing a solitary statement about her situation and her duty.

hinduism_mahabharata_book_3_9647.meaning: Following proper timing and rules helps us achieve our goals without making unnecessary mistakes or errors.
